4e96dc5201:aebc852909511fa6.title: In Wyoming, Are Two Homestead Exemptions Enough?
4e96dc5201:aebc852909511fa6.author: Jared Walczak
4e96dc5201:aebc852909511fa6.summary: No one enjoys paying taxes, but the property tax serves an important purpose, and Wyoming has already implemented significant property tax relief. Proposition 1 would undercut local finances to a degree that would likely force reliance on worse taxes (local or state) and prompt spending cuts that reduce homeowners’ property values.

4e96dc5201:920baa949146f0f0.title: Options to Reform the Tax Treatment of Exempt Hospitals
4e96dc5201:920baa949146f0f0.author: Garrett Watson, Andrew Lautz
4e96dc5201:920baa949146f0f0.summary: Nearly half of all hospitals are exempt from paying US corporate income taxes. As healthcare spending rises, lawmakers have questioned whether hospitals are providing as much in community benefits as they derive from tax exemptions.

4e96dc5201:716970fe74994e9a.title: Expensing Concentrates the Corporate Tax Burden on Economic Profits
4e96dc5201:716970fe74994e9a.author: Erica York
4e96dc5201:716970fe74994e9a.summary: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) improved the corporate tax system with permanent bonus depreciation for machinery and equipment investment and immediate expensing for research and development (R&D) costs.

4e96dc5201:870a3429c65c4564.title: 2026 Economics Nobel Laureate Robert Hall Helped Lay Foundation for Pro-Growth Tax Reform
4e96dc5201:870a3429c65c4564.author: Garrett Watson
4e96dc5201:870a3429c65c4564.summary: Hall’s research helped economists understand how taxes distort investment decisions, while his work with Rabushka shows how to minimize those distortions.

4e96dc5201:0a44cf937245d1bf.title: The California Billionaire Tax’s Ever-Shifting Goalposts
4e96dc5201:0a44cf937245d1bf.author: Daniel Bunn, Dr. Jeff Hoopes
4e96dc5201:0a44cf937245d1bf.summary: Wealth taxes have been a failure everywhere they’ve been tried, which may be why advocates for the California amendment are saying this is a new frontier. But the countries that have tried this gamble know the frontier well, and they’ve left it in the dust.

4e96dc5201:6ade40ffc2022d76.title: Amendment 3: A Restructuring of Florida’s Local Tax Base
4e96dc5201:6ade40ffc2022d76.author: Nicole Fox
4e96dc5201:6ade40ffc2022d76.summary: Florida has long maintained one of the nation’s most competitive state tax codes, but a fundamental change proposed by Amendment 3 could undermine that competitiveness.

4e96dc5201:4399dc08af6acb7b.title: International Tax Competitiveness Index 2026
4e96dc5201:4399dc08af6acb7b.author: Alex Mengden, Luis Zarka
4e96dc5201:4399dc08af6acb7b.summary: While there are many factors that affect a country's economic performance, taxes play an important role. A well-structured tax code is easy for taxpayers to comply with and can promote economic development while raising sufficient revenue for a government’s priorities.

4e96dc5201:239e6b8d4ed8ebac.title: Washington Voters Will Decide Whether to Keep or Reject an Income Tax on High Earners
4e96dc5201:239e6b8d4ed8ebac.author: Jared Walczak
4e96dc5201:239e6b8d4ed8ebac.summary: Washington’s new income tax on high earners doesn’t take effect until 2028, but it is already generating a lot of activity. A measure on the ballot this November, Initiative 645, would reverse the legislature’s decision, preventing the new tax from taking effect.

4e96dc5201:e4bd83d206d5ffb2.title: Spain’s Transformation After a Decade of Fiscal Competition
4e96dc5201:e4bd83d206d5ffb2.author: Cristina Enache
4e96dc5201:e4bd83d206d5ffb2.summary: The 2026 Spanish Regional Tax Competitiveness Index (RTCI) highlights a growing divergence between regions that have embraced tax reform and those whose tax systems have remained largely unchanged.

4e96dc5201:57c0f4b55261d9af.title: Why the US Needs a Fiscal Commission to Help Solve the Debt Crisis
4e96dc5201:57c0f4b55261d9af.author: William McBride
4e96dc5201:57c0f4b55261d9af.summary: The federal government’s debt burden and interest on the debt are near record levels and headed higher, raising legitimate concerns about an eventual debt crisis. Given the increasingly dysfunctional budget process, the most viable option on the table to stave off such a crisis is a statutory bipartisan fiscal commission with buy-in from leaders of both parties.

4e96dc5201:2dd4f3902e2222d6.title: Rental Cars Shouldn’t Face Another Layer of Tax
4e96dc5201:2dd4f3902e2222d6.author: Jared Walczak
4e96dc5201:2dd4f3902e2222d6.summary: Imposing sales taxes on rental car companies’ fleet purchases, in addition to the sales and rental car excise taxes levied when those cars are rented, yields double taxation and causes harmful tax pyramiding.

4e96dc5201:ce7995946a1eea1e.title: Estate and Inheritance Taxes by State, 2026
4e96dc5201:ce7995946a1eea1e.author: Nicole Fox
4e96dc5201:ce7995946a1eea1e.summary: In addition to the federal estate tax, which has a top marginal rate of 40 percent, 12 states and the District of Columbia impose estate taxes, while five states levy inheritance taxes.

4e96dc5201:56383b83d290b900.title: Combined State and Federal Corporate Income Tax Rates in 2026
4e96dc5201:56383b83d290b900.author: Garrett Watson, Alex Durante
4e96dc5201:56383b83d290b900.summary: Corporations in the United States pay federal corporate income taxes levied at a 21 percent rate. Forty-four states and D.C. also levy taxes on corporate income, with top marginal rates ranging from 2.5 percent in North Carolina to 11.5 percent in New Jersey.

4e96dc5201:ebad36d11d70ffb0.title: The 2026 Ballot Measures Shaping State Taxes
4e96dc5201:ebad36d11d70ffb0.author: Janelle Fritts, Erica York, Kyle Hulehan, Dan Carvajal
4e96dc5201:ebad36d11d70ffb0.summary: What happens when voters decide tax policy directly? This November, roughly 40 tax measures are on the ballot across 17 states. Some states want higher taxes on top earners, others want to write low rates into their constitutions, and Missouri voters will decide whether to start a fund that could one day replace every state tax.

4e96dc5201:f409e6466e319f34.title: A Small Value-Added Tax Could Pay for Tariff Repeal
4e96dc5201:f409e6466e319f34.author: Erica York
4e96dc5201:f409e6466e319f34.summary: Rather than continuing the Trump administration’s tariff policy, policymakers should explore new solutions that can raise sustainable revenue with fewer distortions, like replacing the tariffs with a value-added tax.

4e96dc5201:0f7e012116b1a0ae.title: Real Property Taxes in Europe, 2026
4e96dc5201:0f7e012116b1a0ae.author: Alex Mengden
4e96dc5201:0f7e012116b1a0ae.summary: High property taxes levied not only on land but also on buildings and structures can discourage investment in infrastructure, which businesses would have to pay additional tax on.

4e96dc5201:0dbe2c353af17076.title: Colorado’s Election Day Choice on Income Taxes
4e96dc5201:0dbe2c353af17076.author: Jared Walczak
4e96dc5201:0dbe2c353af17076.summary: On Election Day, Coloradans will get to decide on two competing measures on income taxes: an initiated statute that would cap income taxes at the current 4.4 percent rate; and a constitutional amendment that would authorize a graduated-rate individual and corporate income tax, paired with an initiated statute setting new rates, with a top rate of 8.4 percent.

4e96dc5201:166f669ede4c7ca0.title: Inflation Costs New Jerseyans More than a Rebate Check
4e96dc5201:166f669ede4c7ca0.author: Janelle Fritts
4e96dc5201:166f669ede4c7ca0.summary: Missing out on a tax rebate check is certainly disheartening, but New Jersey wallets are getting actively drained by an even bigger problem in the tax code: the state’s graduated-rate income tax thresholds don’t change with inflation, either.

4e96dc5201:e11e1d272f4fd58d.title: 2026 Spanish Regional Tax Competitiveness Index
4e96dc5201:e11e1d272f4fd58d.author: Cristina Enache
4e96dc5201:e11e1d272f4fd58d.summary: The 2026 Spanish Regional Tax Competitiveness Index allows policymakers and taxpayers to evaluate and measure how their regions’ tax systems compare.

4e96dc5201:6aff242e0cfae2cf.title: Why Expensing New Rental Housing Is One of the Best Ways to Tackle the Housing Supply Problem
4e96dc5201:6aff242e0cfae2cf.author: Richard DiSalvo
4e96dc5201:6aff242e0cfae2cf.summary: The Rental Housing Investment Act (RHIA) would remove much of that tax penalty by allowing developers of new rental housing to immediately deduct up to $150,000 of cost per unit.

4e96dc5201:a79e5705cbd45fae.title: Top Five Options Guide Reforms to Simplify the Tax Code
4e96dc5201:a79e5705cbd45fae.author: Andrew Lautz
4e96dc5201:a79e5705cbd45fae.summary: Congress has passed some major simplifying reforms in recent years, but the tax code has still grown more complex over the past few decades. New carveouts, savings vehicles, and targeted tax increases would complicate it further.

4e96dc5201:9d08ee9cfd94558f.title: Proposal to Adjust Tax Treatment of Mutual Funds Improves Neutrality in the Tax Code
4e96dc5201:9d08ee9cfd94558f.author: Garrett Watson
4e96dc5201:9d08ee9cfd94558f.summary: The proposed GROWTH Act would make the tax treatment of investment funds more consistent and improve the tax treatment of saving in the US by allowing investors to defer tax on qualifying reinvested capital gains distributions until they sell their fund shares.

4e96dc5201:df4233eb27351ad5.title: Federal Surcharge Drives Another Increase in Wireless Taxes and Fees in 2026
4e96dc5201:df4233eb27351ad5.author: Scott Mackey, Adam Hoffer
4e96dc5201:df4233eb27351ad5.summary: Applying the sales tax, a traditional broad-based consumption tax, is perfectly appropriate, but excessive targeted taxation of wireless services lacks the traditional justifications—a user-pays system or the internalization of social costs—for excise taxation, raising consumer costs and discouraging investment.

4e96dc5201:47b0bafa2edbe03d.title: The Hidden Tariff Burden of Related-Party Trade
4e96dc5201:47b0bafa2edbe03d.author: Emily Kraschel, Alex Durante
4e96dc5201:47b0bafa2edbe03d.summary: Studies have repeatedly shown that US businesses and consumers are bearing a disproportionate share of the tariff burden.

4e96dc5201:d0c64adf84da5480.title: California’s Wealth Tax Explained (And Why It Might Fail)
4e96dc5201:d0c64adf84da5480.author: Jared Walczak, Erica York, Kyle Hulehan, Dan Carvajal
4e96dc5201:d0c64adf84da5480.summary: California's billionaire tax is on the ballot this November, and it raises more questions than answers. From lost government revenue to legal battles that could drag on for years, what would this first-in-the-nation wealth tax actually do?

4e96dc5201:b361ccdd958d1f16.title: Tax Complexity Now Costs the US Economy over $544 Billion Annually
4e96dc5201:b361ccdd958d1f16.author: Alex Muresianu, Guy Cardwell
4e96dc5201:b361ccdd958d1f16.summary: Americans will spend 6.9 billion hours complying with IRS tax filing and reporting requirements in 2026, costing about $387 billion in lost productivity. Including an additional $157 billion in out-of-pocket costs, complying with the federal tax code will cost Americans more than $544 billion this year, over 1.7 percent of GDP.

4e96dc5201:91f749d31c522c4f.title: States’ Nonconformity with Federal Measurements Creates “Barrels” of Compliance Costs
4e96dc5201:91f749d31c522c4f.author: Jacob Macumber-Rosin
4e96dc5201:91f749d31c522c4f.summary: Many states levy taxes on liquids on a per-barrel basis. However, some states define a “barrel” differently than the standard measurement. The landscape of unharmonious units creates complexity and compliance costs for businesses that must pay these taxes in multiple states.

4e96dc5201:6b4ea4d39f572e59.title: Beer Taxes in Europe, 2026
4e96dc5201:6b4ea4d39f572e59.author: Adam Hoffer, Jacob Macumber-Rosin
4e96dc5201:6b4ea4d39f572e59.summary: With much of the continent celebrating Oktoberfest, it is a great time to examine beer taxes across Europe. Hefty beer taxes increase the price consumers pay for their libations.

4e96dc5201:7237670cf5c0c2ee.title: Three Facts Straightening Out the Debate Over Bonus Depreciation
4e96dc5201:7237670cf5c0c2ee.author: Garrett Watson, Erica York
4e96dc5201:7237670cf5c0c2ee.summary: Expensing for capital investment is not a special tax break. Expensing aligns the timing of tax deductions with the timing of actual capital expenditures so that the tax code does not discourage marginal investment projects.

4e96dc5201:2ff6fa338e6849b8.title: Fiscal Sovereignty and Subsidiarity: What the EU’s Tobacco Excise Directive Gets Wrong
4e96dc5201:2ff6fa338e6849b8.author: Adam Hoffer
4e96dc5201:2ff6fa338e6849b8.summary: The European Union’s revised Tobacco Excise Directive (TED) is the latest proposal from Brussels that attempts to replace Member States’ national autonomy with EU subordination. Harmonized policy in pursuit of a low-friction, Single Market is a worthy goal, but over-exporting policy decisions to Brussels will harm many Member States.

4e96dc5201:e1e9765cb7613f3e.title: The Spiraling Cost of Federal Healthcare Subsidies and Carveouts
4e96dc5201:e1e9765cb7613f3e.author: William McBride, Guy Cardwell
4e96dc5201:e1e9765cb7613f3e.summary: The US federal government faces several fiscal challenges in the coming decades, including the growing burden of federal healthcare programs and tax preferences.

4e96dc5201:e1b979db5f454771.title: Options Guide Shows the “No Tax On” Deductions Are Costly and Complex
4e96dc5201:e1b979db5f454771.author: Andrew Lautz, Garrett Watson
4e96dc5201:e1b979db5f454771.summary: The “no tax on” deductions show the drawbacks of using narrowly tailored provisions to provide tax relief.

4e96dc5201:d02c4bad5feaeb66.title: Full Expensing to Be Made Permanent in Canada
4e96dc5201:d02c4bad5feaeb66.author: Alex Mengden, Cristina Enache
4e96dc5201:d02c4bad5feaeb66.summary: On September 15th, Canada announced that full expensing for machinery, equipment, and patent rights will be made permanent and broadened from around 15 percent to two thirds of business capital investment.

4e96dc5201:9d43b979fc5b54b2.title: As Nicotine Pouch Market Grows, States Face Trade-Off Between Tax Revenue and Harm Reduction
4e96dc5201:9d43b979fc5b54b2.author: Adam Hoffer, Jacob Macumber-Rosin
4e96dc5201:9d43b979fc5b54b2.summary: Oral nicotine pouches have rapidly become a popular option for consumers who want nicotine without the harmful combustion and chemicals of traditional cigarettes. As these alternative nicotine products (ANPs) successfully draw smokers to non-combustible nicotine consumption, many states have scrambled to incorporate these new products into their tax regimes.

4e96dc5201:362d9ccf3018d23a.title: Power and Tax Policy: When Does Leveraging Market Access as a Coercive Geoeconomic Tool Succeed?
4e96dc5201:362d9ccf3018d23a.author: Sean Bray

40c94f9b29:83e72c7055498ecf.title: Lives Wasted and Well-Lived: David Wolpe on The Death of Ivan Ilyich

40c94f9b29:0c24df0751808b58.title: A Nobel for Microfoundations
40c94f9b29:0c24df0751808b58.summary: This year, the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, colloquially called the Nobel Prize in Economics , went to Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University for their work in “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization.” Those five words do not adequately describe their contributions. Hall and Woodford are macroeconomists whose major works emerged when macro was in crisis. Old school Keynesian economics had dominated economic policy discussions since the 1940s. Generally speaking, Keynesians advocated fiscal policy tools (specifically taxes and spending) to stabilize the economy. For about 20 years, those tools seemed to work. But starting in the late 1960s and through the 70s, the macroeconomic relationships broke down. A seemingly impossible confluence of rising inflation and high unemployment characterized this period. Keynesian spending policies were becoming impotent. Critics of Keynesianism rose, and macroeconomics called out for new theories. It was during this period that macroeconomics began to explore more microfoundations. That is, rather than treating the economy as a series of aggregates and their relations to one another, economists started to explore how aggregate macroeconomic factors were the results of individual behavior, institutions, and expectations. Stabilization policy could not be simply levers pulled or pushed by the policymaker. Rather, stabilization policy had to include theories on how people will react to such changes, as well as their expectations about the future. Models such as rational expectations, adaptive expectations, and the permanent income hypothesis were developed during this period as a means to explain why these Keynesian stabilization policies failed. One of the models that came out of this period was Milton Friedman’s Permanent Income Hypothesis. The basic idea is that people base their consumption decisions not just on current income…

40c94f9b29:a780bf86d4a4f4b9.title: The Great Fertility Collapse (with Jesus Fernandez-Villaverde)
40c94f9b29:a780bf86d4a4f4b9.summary: For the first time in human history, we’re not having enough children to keep the world’s population from falling. And fertility is collapsing fastest not in rich nations but in places like Colombia, Thailand, and Guatemala, upending decades of economic wisdom. Economist Jesus Fernandez-Villaverde tells EconTalk’s Russ Roberts that falling fertility has accelerated sharply over the past decade and defies easy explanation. Declining religiosity, smartphones and social media, soaring housing costs, and changing gender norms are popular, but unconfirmed, theories. Fernandez-Villaverde offers his own speculative answer, that modern life makes a third child costly and childlessness easy, but admits the puzzle is unsolved. What’s clearer is why it matters: as retirees become the dominant voting bloc, spending on pensions and health care crowds out roads, schools, and defense. Shrinking economies make public debt harder to service, and fewer births mean fewer scientists, artists, and inventors. (1 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:a54c6f82e5753273.title: Debt and Profit
40c94f9b29:a54c6f82e5753273.summary: An ordinary person can earn a paycheque, pay her taxes, cover living costs and mortgage payments, and perhaps even add to her savings — and at the end of the day she will still owe most of her mortgage. This is a normal state of affairs, and nobody finds it puzzling. Yet when a company reports profits alongside large amounts of debt, the reaction is often to question whether it’s really making money. After all, if a company is “truly” profitable, why is it in debt? The short answer is that debt is not the opposite of profit. Loss is the opposite of profit. This imagined contradiction is easier to resolve once we recognize that profit is a flow and debt is a stock. According to the SEC’s guide to financial statements, the income statement records revenues, expenses, and profit over a period, while the balance sheet records assets and liabilities — such as debt — at a point in time. In fact, debt and profit are entirely unrelated concepts. Imagine a firm borrows money to purchase a machine. When the loan arrives, the firm’s cash and debt rise by the same amount. When the purchase is made, the firm simply exchanges one asset (cash) for another (the machine). Neither transaction creates a profit or a loss. Over time, the machine may be used in productive activities that raise revenue. By the same token, depreciation in the machine’s value can lower profit over its useful life, and interest — the cost of managing debt — adds to expenditures for as long as the debt is outstanding. The best way to think about debt is as a contract that moves purchasing power across people and time. Savers give up control over their resources today, while borrowers promise principal and interest later in exchange for controlling those resources now. Banks and bond markets pool and match funds from many people, letting a single firm undertake a factory, railway, or phone network without first accumulating the cash itself. As Frédéric Bastiat put it, credit institutions “can make it easier…

40c94f9b29:b79d2bc5c55e544a.title: Addiction, Faith, and the Limits of Willpower (with Meghan O’Gieblyn)
40c94f9b29:b79d2bc5c55e544a.summary: Why do we keep doing things we know we shouldn’t? And is that really a failure of will? Author Meghan O’Gieblyn spent years trying to answer that question, first in response to her struggle with alcoholism and her loss of faith, and then by means of Simone Weil, William James, and Iris Murdoch, who argue that the will is powerless over the things we want to change most. Listen as she speaks with EconTalk’s Russ Roberts about her new memoir, Will and Attention , which explores why paying attention does what effort alone can’t, why we can reason ourselves into doing destructive things, and why the choices that most shape our lives are the “choices in between the choices,” or the ones we barely notice making at all. (0 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:e8f93f2515871ba5.title: Prices as a Map for Minds That Can’t Know Everything
40c94f9b29:e8f93f2515871ba5.summary: Reading Dean Ball’s recent essay “ On the Loose ” has me thinking about an old idea in a new light. Ball asks us to imagine a world containing “self-sovereign” AI agents. These are not simply chatbots we rent by the month. They are agents capable of operating independently, acquiring the computer they need to keep running, moving across infrastructure, and interacting economically without a human owner making each decision. Some might be productive. Some, Ball worries, might be rogue. Whether or not you find the whole scenario plausible, it forces an interesting economic question. If such an agent existed, how would it find its way around an economy? It cannot read the minds of the millions of strangers whose choices determine what is valuable. It does not automatically know that a mine flooded yesterday, that a restaurant has empty tables tonight, or that a particular programmer suddenly has three free hours. What can it see? The answer, I think, is the same thing you and I look at: prices. In 1945, Friedrich Hayek published “ The Use of Knowledge in Society .” His starting point was humility about how little any single mind can hold. A modern economy needs to make use of knowledge about who needs tin, which mine just flooded, and what resources happen to be sitting idle in one particular place. This information is not sitting in a central file. It is scattered across millions of people, most of whom know only their own small corner of the world. Hayek emphasized the importance of knowledge of the particular circumstances of “time and place.” The person standing beside an underused machine knows something that a central planner does not. Hayek’s insight was that the price system allows people to act on some of this knowledge without possessing all of it. When tin becomes scarce, its price rises. The people who use tin do not need to know why. It could be a flooded mine or a war in a country they cannot find on a map. They only need to know that tin is more…

40c94f9b29:36c6ccbb0c4202cf.title: Public Choice and Politics Without Romance (with Mike Munger)

40c94f9b29:b1746ff0fc72856e.title: The Constitution of Liberty in the Era of AI
40c94f9b29:b1746ff0fc72856e.summary: We are living through a great social transformation comparable to the industrial revolution. What sets it apart is not only its magnitude, but its multidimensional convergence: technological, economic, political, and epistemic shifts unfolding simultaneously and reinforcing one another. This shift places growing strain on inherited political cleavages and ideological frameworks, many forged under very different technological and institutional conditions. Mega-trends such as digitalization, artificial intelligence, platform economies, biotechnology, and the reconfiguration of global networks are not just reshaping production and exchange; they are redefining the conditions under which governance operates. The result is a systemic transformation that penetrates the foundations of contemporary political and economic orders. At the core of this transformation is a radical expansion of the institutional possibility frontier. Technological change does not merely enhance existing arrangements; it reshapes what is feasible, enabling new forms of coordination, monitoring, enforcement, and collective decision-making that were previously impractical or unimaginable. As a result, institutional designs once confined to theory and speculation may now become operationally relevant. What is emerging is not a simple adaptation of existing systems, but a mutation of their underlying architecture. In this context, the central question is: what place, if any, will classical liberal principles, values, and institutional arrangements occupy within this emerging order? Put differently, to what extent do current technological and structural trends constrain, erode, or, alternatively, enable new instantiations of liberal governance along classical lines? And, reciprocally, to what extent can these trends themselves be shaped, redirected, or constitutionally framed by insights derived from the classical liberal tradition? The issue thus becomes operational and strategic. It is not enough…

40c94f9b29:bc61297bc1c18f9d.title: The Cultural Theory of YIMBY
40c94f9b29:bc61297bc1c18f9d.summary: How does anything get built? What are the political precursors to development? Michael Munger has an interesting, and at times persuasive, argument that self-interest combines with particular institutional designs, such as public hearings, to create a prisoner’s dilemma where everyone knows that development is in aggregate desirable but wants that development to be in the next town over. This is, in many ways, the conventional story of NIMBY (not-in-my-backyard) politics. That story isn’t wrong per se, but it’s missing a critical component: culture. The claim that culture matters is sometimes dismissed as hand-wavy or “just vibes,” but it’s critical to understanding whether building is the default or deviant move, to identifying who has standing to object, and to explaining whether a proposed new development is seen as a contribution to the community or a threat to it. Without understanding the cultural ideas that drive NIMBYism, scholars and housing advocates are flying blind in a storm. At the extreme ends of the spectrum, the desirability of land use choices is obvious to the locals. Virtually everyone would welcome a new bakery taking over an abandoned building. No neighborhood wants a new wastewater treatment facility going in next to them. But for all the marginal cases between those two extremes, culture plays a huge role in what and how much gets built. I argue that three cultural practices (growth orientation, property rights norms, and positive-sum attitudes) act essentially as gates. If a place fails on any one of them, it is very likely to underbuild. Development will thus, over time, gravitate toward places that can pass all three of these cultural tests. Growth Orientation There are places where people take pride in growth. Think of this as “growth boosterism.” The town I grew up in (Chelsea, Alabama) had a strong dose of this. Any time a new business got started, people were excited: “Hey, did you see we have a Mexican restaurant now? How cool is…

40c94f9b29:73444ee645afd804.title: Put It in Your Own Backyard
40c94f9b29:73444ee645afd804.summary: On a chilly Thursday evening last December, citizens in Dorr, Michigan, a small community about a half-hour south of Grand Rapids, attended a town hall meeting to discuss the possible construction of a data center on the north end of town. Some of the attendees came from families who had lived in Dorr for generations and, worried about the disruptions posed by a new data center, came ready to defend their town. Instead, to their dismay, they discovered the township supervisor had, without a public hearing, already signed an agreement. Microsoft, never bothering to send a representative to meet the public, now held the deed to more than 250 acres of prime farmland, an arrangement citizens knew nothing about until everything was signed and sealed. With the land already sold and the ink dry, the citizens’ impotence turned to repressed rage. I say “repressed” because the citizens have not, as yet, taken matters into their own hands. To my knowledge, no lawsuits have been filed, pitchforks wielded, or Sabo-tabbies unleashed. No doubt the nameless and faceless drones at Microsoft had bemused looks on their faces as the citizens of Dorr organized their seemingly pointless protests. After all, what mattered Dorr’s 7,900 souls when progress was at stake? So what if that little town was sacrificed on the altar of Big Tech? One imagines a Microsoft exec in his Seattle high-rise pulling on a cigar, a martini in his other hand, smiling smugly at the thought of a small group of Michiganders thinking they could stop the course of history itself. It doesn’t bother me that Dorr, Michigan, doesn’t matter to the executives at Microsoft; what bothers me is that it bothers those executives that Dorr matters to the people who live there. Dorr is just one of those “middle-of-nowhere” places to which people stubbornly cling, places where, for generations, people have lived and loved and raised families and built communities and buried their dead. Who would deign to defend such places…

40c94f9b29:c9412abc338f9cea.title: The Death of Reading (with James Marriott)
40c94f9b29:c9412abc338f9cea.summary: Are we living in the new Dark Ages? Despite vast technological advances, our societies are increasingly looking like those that preceded the advent of literacy. So argues journalist James Marriott , who sees in our abandonment of reading a threat to democracy and a reversal of many of the Enlightenment’s gains. He and EconTalk’s Russ Roberts trace literacy from its fragile first days in ancient Mesopotamia through to the printing press and the “Reading Revolution” of the mid-to-late 18th century, exploring how–and whether–its spread shaped major historical events. They analyze Marriott’s claim that reading grounds politics in rationality, consider the role of the Republic of Letters in driving Europe’s Industrial Revolution, and debate whether a book or a movie is better at conveying complexity. Marriott ends with a consolation: Just as fast food gave rise to the gym, informational junk food may give rise to reading as an intentional discipline. (0 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:6a811fa2b327bf0f.title: AI and the Luddites
40c94f9b29:6a811fa2b327bf0f.summary: Daron Acemoglu has been the target of an unusually harsh piece in The Economist , which prompted fellow economists to come to his aid. The magazine cast doubt on the data and methods underlying his research on institutions; it suggested that Acemoglu frames complex historical episodes through overly simple narratives, and that “institutions” in his hands is a category elastic enough to explain anything; and it dismissed his position on AI as “pessimistic to the point of losing their credibility.” Acemoglu called the article a hit piece and has replied , objecting among other things that the verdict rests on the testimony of economists the magazine did not name. Most of those who came to his defense questioned the very idea that a magazine could challenge the scientific output of one of the most prominent social scientists of his generation—and a Nobel laureate. This is a curious line of defense, and an old one. Guilds have always held that a craft can be judged only from inside it. Among those who joined the debate is Luigi Zingales of the University of Chicago. In a post on X , Zingales—who has himself “criticized important parts of Daron’s work”—framed the controversy as a by-product of a disagreement over AI, or more precisely as a kind of exemplary punishment meted out by The Economist to a very prominent AI critic: “Everybody has heard of the Luddites, but few know Sir Thomas Maitland, the man who defeated them. Rather than using brute force to take them all out, Maitland simply identified the men he took to be ringleaders, had them arrested on evidence that was often thin, and executed them. Hit one, educate a hundred. This is the strategy that the British magazine The Economist seems to have adopted toward the new version of the Luddites: AI critics.” The sentence bears two readings: that AI critics are the new Luddites, or merely that they are being treated as such. The weaker reading turns the post into a complaint about tone, which would be a waste of a…

40c94f9b29:875ba4b08d99c2ca.title: Incentives Are for Losers (with Adam Mastroianni)
40c94f9b29:875ba4b08d99c2ca.summary: Incentives matter, sure. But what should you do when following the incentives means quietly participating in something wrong? Psychologist Adam Mastroianni argues that obeying bad incentives–shading a headline for clicks, keeping the found wallet because no one’s watching–is “loser behavior,” a surrender of the hardest and most human task: figuring out right from wrong for yourself. In this wide-ranging EconTalk conversation, he and Russ Roberts explore Le Guin’s “Omelas,” the “big fish” you glimpse that could upend your whole life, and Charles Sumner’s near-fatal courage. They wrestle with whether good incentives or good people matter more, why lavish academic salaries may attract exactly the wrong scholars, and the moral lessons of marriage. (2 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:cf373a1276460339.title: The Economist Who Forgot Economics
40c94f9b29:cf373a1276460339.summary: Daron Acemoglu won the Nobel Prize in economics in 2024 and is the third most cited economist of all time. Thus, the paradox of his new book, What Happened to Liberal Democracy? , is that its most serious analytic failures are economic. He provides a sincere and serious consideration of modern liberalism’s estrangement from the working class. But when he moves from description to solutions, the basic building blocks of economic analysis disappear. Imperfect markets are compared with an idealized government. Expansive agencies are proposed while the risk of their capture—well known in public-choice theory—is ignored. And while Acemoglu is known for integrating institutions into economics, he sometimes celebrates democratic consensus without attention to the elite institutions that formed it. Acemoglu “pitches his tent” on the left side of liberalism, arguing that it “has historically been an engine of material and social progress.” Today he believes tradition should give birth to “working-class liberalism,” which means, for him, creating a more level economic playing field and technological change that complements rather than displaces labor. The book is well-intentioned. He recognizes that elites cannot be trusted to direct culture. But he never explains why they can be trusted to direct technology, redistribution, and the administrative state. Acemoglu argues that the postindustrial economy puts a premium on cognitive skills useful in fields such as elevating finance, health, and education, while reducing the importance of manufacturing. He claims that automation “severs the link between mass production and shared prosperity” and has resulted in “the disappearance of good jobs for workers without a college degree.” Acemoglu thus endorses the economic explanation for populist discontent popular among left-liberals. What is original about his account is his willingness to also highlight the contribution of left-liberals to working-class alienation. As in my own…

40c94f9b29:304b39b783c97a3a.summary: Daron Acemoglu won the Nobel Prize in economics in 2024 and is the third most cited economist of all time. 26e942feef:42da307b91160128.title: Representation over Rents: Sorting in a Market for Lemons
26e942feef:42da307b91160128.author: Pieter Gautier
26e942feef:42da307b91160128.summary: Search frictions normally raise the bar for sorting: both random and directed search require complementarities strictly stronger than the supermodularity that suffices in Becker's (1973) frictionless model. We introduce private information into this setting: firms post wages without observing worker productivity, while better workers have better outside options, creating a market for lemons (Akerlof 1970). We show that this information friction pushes sorting the other way: attracting high-productivity workers without attracting low-productivity ones requires a higher wage paired with a lower job-finding probability, so vacancies fill faster. This strict ranking of vacancy filling rates sorts the market positively whenever output is complementary in worker and firm quality. Becker's condition therefore suffices once more, and private information makes positive sorting easier to sustain than complete information does.

26e942feef:cfa2403e9f8860ee.title: Returns to Private Debt in Emerging and Developing Economies
26e942feef:cfa2403e9f8860ee.author: Moelders, Florian
26e942feef:cfa2403e9f8860ee.summary: Private debt is an important form of corporate financing in emerging markets, but its investor returns are not well understood. This paper uses loan-level cash flow data from the International Finance Corporation to provide the first systematic evidence on realized returns across 4, 109 loans over more than 20 years, totaling about US$115 billion in 127 countries. Post–global financial crisis loans outperform both the JPMorgan Corporate Emerging Market Bond Index and U.S. Treasuries, with public market equivalents of 1.02 and 1.10, respectively, rising to 1.05 and 1.14 over the latest five years. Over 2002–24, the corresponding public market equivalents are 0.98 and 1.07, respectively, with global financial crisis–era vintages posting weaker performance relative to the JPMorgan Corporate Emerging Market Bond Index. Overall, returns are competitive with public markets. The paper also assesses financial performance more specifically within the most challenging markets: very low-income countries and fragile and conflict-affected states. Although default rates are higher in these markets, returns relative to public-market alternatives are statistically indistinguishable from those of the overall portfolio, suggesting that the International Finance Corporation priced default risk appropriately even in these markets.

26e942feef:7d35b3deb708c512.title: Minimum Wages and Cost-Push Inflation: Economy-Wide Evidence from Germany
26e942feef:7d35b3deb708c512.author: Maximilian Priem
26e942feef:7d35b3deb708c512.summary: We provide the first estimates of minimum wage effects on the aggregate price level using data on the near-full German consumer basket across four national reforms, 2015-2024. Drawing on a structural model of pricing under imperfect competition, we utilise minimum wage cost shocks rather than the commonly used firm-level ‘bite’ that we show to be biased under strategic complementarity. Labour cost pass-through is 83-94 percent, at the higher end of estimates for other cost shocks. The implied macro-price elasticity is 0.024. The largest increase in October 2022 to €12 raised the aggregate price level by 0.39 percent.

26e942feef:0b2ff47be3072c71.title: Moving Out: Geoeconomic Policy and the Relocation of Foreign Affiliates
26e942feef:0b2ff47be3072c71.author: Stefano Verzillo
26e942feef:0b2ff47be3072c71.summary: Governments increasingly use trade and industrial policy to reshape where multinationals produce, yet standard measures of this geoeconomic pressure are aggregate and cannot detect origin-specific discrimination. We build a bilateral, directional index of relative protectionism that measures how restrictive a destination is toward a given origin. We combine it with bilateral geopolitical risk indices and global ownership links over the period 2010-21, and estimate a gravity-type Poisson-Pseudo Maximum Likelihood model with three-way fixed effects. Our results show that where bilateral protectionism is greater, foreign-affiliate presence is markedly smaller: a 1 percentage point increase in the index is associated with 1.3% fewer subsidiaries than that origin-destination pair would otherwise have. The main mechanism runs through an operational hostility channel (e.g. discriminatory subsidies, procurement exclusion), which outweighs an offsetting tariff-jumping channel and concentrates in non-tradable sectors, where serving the market requires local presence. The estimates show no evidence of anticipation and are robust to longer lags and sample splits. Bilateral geopolitical risk enters with the same negative sign, adding a smaller but complementary layer of fragmentation risk to the effect of geoeconomic policy.

26e942feef:28297616f008c815.title: The Production Network Amplification of Retaliatory Tariffs
26e942feef:28297616f008c815.author: Jacob Short
26e942feef:28297616f008c815.summary: We develop a framework to quantify how tariff changes on imported goods affect sectoral and aggregate consumption prices through direct and production-network channels. Using Canada's input-output matrix and administrative firm-good import data for the universe of Canadian firms, we estimate price elasticities for tariffs on U.S.-imported goods. Tariffs on machinery and equipment and transport equipment generate the largest effects on final prices, reflecting their widespread use as intermediate inputs. On average, two-thirds of the total price response stems from higher intermediate input costs passing through domestic supply chains. Applying the framework to Canada's 2025 counter-tariffs, we estimate consumption price increases of 1.56 and 0.72 percentage points for the pre- and post-September 2025 phases, respectively; alternative packages of equal import value could reduce aggregate price effects by three to seven times. A hypothetical CUSMA breakdown reverting to MFN tariffs would raise final-good prices by 0.64 percentage points.

26e942feef:f8f5a1c2dbabd23e.title: Beliefs Over Contracts
26e942feef:f8f5a1c2dbabd23e.author: Collin B. Raymond
26e942feef:f8f5a1c2dbabd23e.summary: We study how firms choose among incentive contracts and how accurately managers predict their effects. Using a survey of managerial beliefs and a large-scale field experiment, we randomly assign agents at the market level to several widely used, expenditure-equivalent incentive schemes. In the field, the best-performing contract increases agent output and firm revenue by over 20% relative to the status quo, despite being ranked lower by managers, whereas the worst-performing contract performs as predicted. Managers correctly identify underperforming contracts but systematically underestimate top- performing ones. We document the sources of performance di!erences—labor supply responses rather than selection or pricing and the determinants of managerial predictability: contract complexity and managerial hierarchy. Our results highlight the importance of contract design for firm performance and reveal systematic limits to managerial cognition in shaping incentives.

26e942feef:334d09e6e7f7fdb7.title: The Investment Channel of Monetary Policy: Disentangling Firm Heterogeneity
26e942feef:334d09e6e7f7fdb7.author: Laura Pilossoph
26e942feef:334d09e6e7f7fdb7.summary: To study monetary policy transmission at the firm level, researchers typically consider heterogeneity along a small number of firm characteristics, such as size or leverage. We instead estimate the full distribution of firms’ investment responses to monetary policy, using a clustering regression framework. Our novel approach captures multidimensional and unobservable heterogeneity across firms and time. We find that investment by most firms in most time periods responds little to monetary policy. Only about 5% of firm-time observations are associated with a strong response. We then investigate the sources of heterogeneity ex post. We find that most of the variation in investment sensitivity arises within firms over time. Although several firm characteristics predict responsiveness to monetary policy, the majority of heterogeneity remains unexplained by firm observables. We demonstrate that our empirical estimates provide new targets for disciplining structural models of firm heterogeneity.

26e942feef:c11ab353728739f8.title: Taxing Entrepreneurial Wealth: Evidence from Norway, 2021–2025
26e942feef:c11ab353728739f8.author: Marius A. K. Ring
26e942feef:c11ab353728739f8.summary: Whether imposing higher taxes on business owners adversely affects business activity by constraining investment and inducing capitalist flight is a central question in the ongoing debate on how to tax the ultra wealthy. To shed new light, I exploit a series of related Norwegian reforms during 2021–2024 that increased dividend tax rates, removed migration-related capital gains tax loopholes, and nearly doubled the effective marginal tax rate on business wealth. These reforms spurred international debate and, allegedly, an “exodus” of Norwegian billionaires (Financial Times, 2023). While I document clear effects on migration, these responses are concentrated among the top 0.1% of the wealth distribution and mostly confined to 2022 and 2023. My results indicate that at most 100 individuals left due to the reforms. I find no evidence of significant outmigration or reduced inflows of startup founders or inventors. I estimate that absent any outmigration, wealth tax revenues would have increased by 75% from 2021 to 2024. Reform-driven outmigration lowers the revenue gain to 71.5%. My findings further show that outmigrating owners’ firms remain economically active and do not reduce investment. In a broader set of analyses, I examine whether business outcomes are affected, regardless of whether owners outmigrate, since firms may reduce investment both due to liquidity constraints or distortions to owners’ savings decisions. I compare firms owned by Norwegian individuals subject to the wealth tax with firms owned by foreigners and other tax-exempt entities. By merging historical ownership data from Orbis with the Norwegian shareholder register, I perform these analyses on both Norwegian and foreign-domiciled firms. Across settings, I find no evidence that Norwegian-owned firms pay out more dividends or invest less after the reforms, nor is there any evidence that the reform induced more bankruptcies. These findings indicate that the short-run economic costs of wealth…

26e942feef:29ebb44ed7b384e0.title: When Does Bad News Stick? Topic-Level Asymmetry in Narrative Dynamics
26e942feef:29ebb44ed7b384e0.author: Eswar S. Prasad
26e942feef:29ebb44ed7b384e0.summary: When does bad news stick? This paper shows that the persistence of media sentiment depends not only on whether news is good or bad, but also on what the news is about. Using the complete Wall Street Journal archive from 1990 to 2025, we construct monthly positive and negative sentiment indices for twelve economic topics and estimate topic-specific sentiment dynamics. Bad-news innovations generate larger cumulative responses than positive-sentiment innovations in every topic, indicating that negativity asymmetry is a broad feature of media sentiment. But the size of this asymmetry varies sharply across topics. The bad-minus-positive persistence gap is largest in security and human rights, firms and corporate strategy, health and public safety, and real estate and financial stability. Bad-news persistence is also sizable in data-rich topics such as financial markets, real estate, and corporate news, suggesting that frequent information arrival does not necessarily lead narratives to revert quickly. These findings show that aggregate sentiment indices mask substantial topic-level heterogeneity in the asymmetric dynamics of narratives, with potential implications for how persistent negative sentiment shapes expectations, asset prices, and real economic outcomes.

26e942feef:833c47310195d6e4.title: Integration versus Outsourcing with Vertical Linkages
26e942feef:833c47310195d6e4.author: Gaetano Alfredo Minerva
26e942feef:833c47310195d6e4.summary: I propose a mechanism for the coexistence of vertical integration and outsourcing within an industry. In a monopolistically competitive model with incomplete contracts, final-good producers under either organizational form combine labor and differentiated inputs to produce fixed capital. Since its unit cost depends on the industry price index, distinct zero-profit conditions can hold, sustaining a mixed free-entry equilibrium. The forms differ in fixed-capital cost per unit of contribution to the price index; this ranking determines comparative statics and whether local stability is possible. I derive a sufficient condition ensuring stability whenever the mixed equilibrium exists. In numerical parameterizations using empirically standard elasticities of substitution, the condition holds throughout the admissible range of vertical-linkage intensity. Within the stable region, larger markets raise the integrated share without changing output prices or supplier bargaining terms. Relative firm size depends on governance costs and upstream bargaining share, so the model imposes no uniform ranking.

26e942feef:412b5df697ac2708.title: Avoiding Regulation: Evidence from Nursing Homes
26e942feef:412b5df697ac2708.author: Riley League
26e942feef:412b5df697ac2708.summary: We study strategic responses by firms to threshold-based regulations. We document extensive bunching in response to additional staffing requirements for California nursing homes with at least 100 beds. To estimate the regulation’s effect on staffing, we develop a novel treatment effects estimator for threshold-based regulations under precise manipulation, by decomposing firms into response types based on counterfactual and realized staffing and size, separating causal effects from selection. We estimate that higher staffing above the threshold is nearly entirely due to selection, with low-staffing facilities manipulating their size to avoid the regulation. These size distortions limit access, particularly for disadvantaged patients.

26e942feef:efbecc19f108fc0e.title: Regulating a Monopolist through Capacity Control
26e942feef:efbecc19f108fc0e.author: Dihan Zou
26e942feef:efbecc19f108fc0e.summary: We study monopoly regulation when capacity is contractible but subsequent output is not. A firm privately observes its production cost before installing costly capacity and then choosing output, while the regulator cannot use transfers. We provide sufficient conditions under which a single capacity floor implements an optimal mechanism with full participation. The floor raises output by changing investment while leaving utilization to the firm after installation costs are sunk. Under additional conditions, the allocation has three regions: laissez-faire, full utilization of the floor, and underutilization. High-cost types knowingly install capacity they will not fully use, yet produce more than under laissez-faire. This physical waste is a necessary evil of optimal regulation that expands service. We also show that underutilization can persist in optimal regulation with capacity-contingent subsidies or a common entry fee.

26e942feef:dd05b757bdca93b4.title: Financing the AI Buildout
26e942feef:dd05b757bdca93b4.author: Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh
26e942feef:dd05b757bdca93b4.summary: Artificial intelligence is driving a large expansion in data center capacity, power infrastructure, and specialized computing equipment. We estimate that a 1 GW AI campus costs about $41 billion. A 188 GW U.S. buildout completed by 2032 would require total investment of nearly$9 trillion and amount to annual investment of 3.2 percent of GDP over 2025–2032. As hyperscaler capital expenditures outgrow internal cash flow, financing is shifting toward leases, joint ventures, project debt, private credit, securitization, and special-purpose vehicles. These structures expand funding capacity but also raise asset-level leverage, obscure contingent obligations, and expose investors to tenant concentration, technological obsolescence, execution delays, and uncertain residual values.

26e942feef:50e9468ebde11262.title: Which Workers Left the Labor Force Post-COVID Recession and Why?: Filing, Tax Credit Take-Up, and Labor Force Engagement by Occupation
26e942feef:50e9468ebde11262.author: Michael Stevens
26e942feef:50e9468ebde11262.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic caused a sharp initial rise in unemployment, followed by an unexpectedly tight labor market. Using a panel of tax data containing newly assembled information on worker occupation, we document persistent labor force exit, especially among low-income and low-skill workers. Low-skilled unmarried men are by far the most likely to exit, reinforcing recent concerns regarding the economic and social engagement of this group. Contrary to prevailing theories, we find little evidence that school closures, virus exposure, stimulus payments, or unemployment benefits explain these exits. Nor is the exit explained by additional upgrading of occupations or firm quality. Individuals who leave the labor force do not (on average) make up the missing income; however, self-employment income replaces roughly a quarter of the lost W-2 income. The facts suggest that the willingness to work for low pay decreased and preferences for leisure and job flexibility increased among a large set of workers who have found ways to get by with less income. These results have implications for tax policy, fiscal projections, and labor market dynamics in the post-pandemic economy.

26e942feef:3bfb18e406fc8d9c.title: Same Destination, Different Eyes: FDI and Trade Responses to Media Coverage of Geopolitical Risk
26e942feef:3bfb18e406fc8d9c.author: Yasuyuki Todo
26e942feef:3bfb18e406fc8d9c.summary: Existing measures of geopolitical risk are country-level and assume that all investors face the same risk in a given destination. This paper constructs a directional, bilateral geopolitical risk index that captures how the domestic media of each source country report on geopolitical conflicts involving each destination country. Using GDELT news data, the index covers more than 200 source and destination countries at a monthly frequency. We combine the index with project-level data on greenfield FDI and product-level trade data, and exploit variation across source countries for the same destination and period while controlling for destination-specific shocks. Source countries whose media place greater emphasis on a destination's geopolitical risk subsequently announce more greenfield projects there: a one-standard-deviation increase in the index is associated with a 7% increase in new projects. This suggests that firms may read such coverage as a signal of future market-access frictions and localize production in advance. Consistent with this interpretation, the association is concentrated in projects serving the host market and in sectors that depend on local demand, and is absent among politically aligned country pairs. By contrast, higher risk coverage is followed by a short-lived decline in imports, driven by severe conflicts, while exports do not respond.

26e942feef:8f4b54a02b7d1905.title: Tax Planning and Multinational Behavior
26e942feef:8f4b54a02b7d1905.author: Juan Carlos Suárez Serrato
26e942feef:8f4b54a02b7d1905.summary: We use newly linked IRS data to study how US multinationals use tax-planning structures that exploit mismatches between US and foreign tax laws. In 2016, these structures accounted for 36% of foreign profits despite being adopted by only 18% of firms. We develop and estimate a structural model using adoption patterns and changes in foreign effective tax rates, domestic and foreign investment, and global R&D following adoption. The model implies substantial heterogeneity in adoption costs and benefits and shows that restricting tax planning creates tradeoffs between tax revenue and economic activity that are amplified by global R&D linkages.

26e942feef:e0f0f748cc34a0ff.title: How Low Can You Go? Validating Administrative Union Records for Substate Estimates of US Union Membership
26e942feef:e0f0f748cc34a0ff.author: Eric Thai
26e942feef:e0f0f748cc34a0ff.summary: Unions are important economic and political actors at the local level, but the primary source on US union membership, the Current Population Survey (CPS), is unreliable below the state level. Researchers have therefore turned to union-reported membership in federal "LM" filings, geolocating unions and aggregating their reported membership to estimate union density for counties, commuting zones, and congressional districts. We ask whether this practice is sound. We develop and defend multilevel regression with poststratification (MrP) on the CPS as a benchmark, then validate LM-based estimates against it from the state level down. LM, CPS, and MrP are highly correlated at the state level, but this correlation is roughly halved at the congressional-district, commuting-zone, and county levels. The breakdown is driven in part by reporting "lumpiness, " which produces improbable values, including union densities exceeding 100%. Missing public sector union members explains only a small part of this divergence. These issues are substantively consequential: in a standard commuting-zone "China shock" regression, swapping density measures changes the import-exposure coefficient enough to alter its magnitude, significance, and sign. We conclude that LM records remain a rich resource for studying unions as organizations, but aggregating LM-reported membership is not a reliable way to measure union density at fine geographic resolution.

26e942feef:56b8167edcf7b112.title: Company wage policy in a low-wage labor market
26e942feef:56b8167edcf7b112.author: Machin, Stephen
26e942feef:56b8167edcf7b112.summary: We study how firms set wages for their employees when they can legally age discriminate across workers. We exploit an age-specific minimum wage change in the UK, which raised the minimum applying to workers aged 25 and over, leaving unchanged the minima for younger workers. Using matched employer-employee data on a low-paying sector, we show large, positive wage spillovers on workers aged under 25, which arise within firms from company wage policy. Pay equity norms offer the most parsimonious explanation for the emergence of spillovers. The effects that we document also operate in other low-paying sectors of the UK labor market.

26e942feef:a39b8ab0b2dc1a3f.title: Digital Social Pressure, Managerial Decision-Making and Worker Performance: Evidence from Professional Football
26e942feef:a39b8ab0b2dc1a3f.author: James Reade
26e942feef:a39b8ab0b2dc1a3f.summary: Digital platforms expose workers and managers to immediate, public, and persistent evaluations from external audiences, creating a form of social pressure that may shape workplace decisions. We examine whether such digital social pressure predicts subsequent opportunity allocation and worker performance, using professional football as a high-frequency empirical setting. We link player-match data from Europeâ€™s five major leagues to post-match Twitter commentary and construct measures of negative sentiment, toxicity, and racial abuse. Comparing players with themselves over time and teammates in the same current match, we find that greater negative sentiment is associated with a lower probability of appearing in the teamâ€™s next match. Toxicity shows a similar but less stable association, while racial-abuse intensity is imprecisely estimated when the measures enter jointly. By contrast, associations with performance conditional on a subsequent appearance are small and imprecise. Overall, the findings suggest that digital social pressure is reflected more strongly in the allocation of subsequent opportunities than in worker performance, showing how public evaluations generated outside formal organizational boundaries can become part of the reputational environment surrounding internal managerial decisions.

26e942feef:3f9f2463ab81f32e.title: Droughts and Firms in Tunisia
26e942feef:3f9f2463ab81f32e.author: Zaveri, Esha Dilip
26e942feef:3f9f2463ab81f32e.summary: Tunisia is among the Mediterranean’s most climate-exposed countries facing acute water scarcity. Although a growing literature has documented the effects of extreme weather on firms, few studies have used longitudinal administrative data to track how business performance evolves over time. This paper draws on about two decades of firm-level records from Tunisia’s formal business registry (Répertoire National des Entreprises), linking firm locations to satellite-based precipitation measures at the delegation level, which is Tunisia’s second-level administrative unit. Using more than 1 million firm-year observations, the study finds that droughts—defined as negative precipitation shocks—reduce total revenues and revenues per worker by approximately 12 and 11 percent, respectively. Large formal firms, non-exporting firms, and domestic firms are disproportionately vulnerable. The results are robust across a range of sensitivity analyses.

26e942feef:f885511e44d1104c.title: More than just Plug and Play: Early Evidence on Organisational Capital and AI Adoption
26e942feef:f885511e44d1104c.author: Riley, Rebecca
26e942feef:f885511e44d1104c.summary: This paper provides early evidence that AI adoption by firms is linked to management practices in unique ways. Using panel data from the UK Management and Expectations Survey (MES), we find that firms with higher baseline management scores are significantly more likely to adopt AI. This relationship is specific to AI: the same management practices show no relationship with the adoption of other technologies such as robotics, specialized equipment, or specialized software. We also find that management capabilities related to performance measurement appear strongly related to AI adoption. These results suggest that organisational complementarities are specific to different technologies, with implications for policies to encourage AI adoption by firms.

26e942feef:cb9cb0f82a495a67.title: Unlocking Firm Innovation in Peripheral Regions: The Critical Role of Local Psychological Openness
26e942feef:cb9cb0f82a495a67.author: Obschonka, Martin
26e942feef:cb9cb0f82a495a67.summary: Firms in peripheral and less knowledge endowed regions often struggle with innovation, as it is deeply rooted in and influenced by local characteristics. Although recent research highlights the significant, yet complex and hard-to-quantify role of local 'soft factors' such as culture and macro-psychology (e.g., local psychological openness) for firm innovation, we know relatively little about its specific role for firms located in the knowledge periphery. This study examines the hypothesis that favorable local soft factors, such as psychological openness, can compensate for unfavorable local hard factors for innovation of firms located in the knowledge periphery. Drawing upon Schmookler's scissor metaphor, we theoretically elaborate how local psychological openness impacts firm innovation by shaping both the demand and supply sides of the innovation process. In our arguments, we also incorporated the contingent impact of both regional (external) and firm (internal) factors on the relationship between local psychological openness and firm innovation. Our empirical investigation of a large and longitudinal sample of Swedish firms across 2004 to 2018 revealed a compensatory effect of local psychological openness for local 'structural knowledge gaps' in less endowed peripheral regions. Implications for research and policymaking addressing innovation in firms and regions are discussed.

26e942feef:ab68125267741376.title: Ideas and Firm Dynamics When It Takes Two to Tango
26e942feef:ab68125267741376.author: Honghao Wang
26e942feef:ab68125267741376.summary: Teams of inventors now produce over 80 percent of U.S. patents, up from just 45 percent in 1976. Over the same period, inventor employment has become increasingly concentrated in large firms, rising six times more than overall employment concentration. To explain these trends, we develop a new model of endogenous team formation within firms and embed it in a general equilibrium model of the inventor labor market. Teams increase firms’ returns to scale by increasing the likelihood of productive matches between inventors. The value of these matches rises over time, possibly driven by increasing knowledge specialization. This causes large firms to expand and small firms to shrink in equilibrium, accounting for the observed increase in inventor employment concentration. Because firms do not internalize knowledge spillovers, there is misallocation of inventors across firms. The rise of team production amplifies this misallocation by a factor of six by reallocating inventors away from small firms that generate disproportionately large knowledge spillovers.

26e942feef:ba15f4b78fc291d8.title: Endogenous Markups and Trade Elasticities
26e942feef:ba15f4b78fc291d8.author: Paulina Restrepo-Echavarria
26e942feef:ba15f4b78fc291d8.summary: We develop a search model of international trade where buyers allocate costly cognitive attention across suppliers. Suppliers exploit the cost of shifting attention to extract markups, giving dominant firms the cushion to absorb cost shocks while marginal suppliers pass them on. Validating this mechanism with U.S. tariff data, we estimate a highly concentrated U.S. domestic market. Consequently, while targeted tariffs spur offshore substitution, blanket tariffs force buyers toward captive domestic monopolies. Incumbents’ growing market power raises markups and halves the aggregate macro elasticity relative to micro estimates. Integrating endogenous market-power-dependent elasticity along the path to autarky more than doubles the U.S. gains from trade compared with standard constant-elasticity predictions.

26e942feef:dec48c50650f2aaa.title: Shipping to America
26e942feef:dec48c50650f2aaa.author: Francesco Zanetti
26e942feef:dec48c50650f2aaa.summary: We study the macroeconomic and trade-policy implications of disruptions to U.S.-bound shipping routes. Standard models treat them as iceberg-cost shocks, conflating the shock with the response to it. Using satellite vessel-tracking data, we construct route-level measures of potential and effective capacity for all U.S.-bound container ships from 2016 to 2025. Utilization losses in recent disruptions ran 20 to 40 percentage points, and began months before port congestion became visible. We embed these measures in a general equilibrium model in which firms reallocate a common fleet without internalizing the congestion they create and price above marginal cost, while importers’ sourcing responds to route profitability. The reallocation triggered by a disruption then has first-order welfare effects, and the route’s Domar weight is not a sufficient statistic for its welfare cost. The 2021 West Coast crisis and the 2023–2024 Red Sea attacks cost 0.69% and 0.35% of output. Naval protection of Red Sea shipping generated benefits of 0.04–0.08% of output at a fiscal cost of 0.02%. Tariffs decongest the routes they tax, offsetting or even reversing their conventional welfare cost.

26e942feef:6ade09d9ef1d30fe.title: The Early Spatial Diffusion of Generative AI in Japan: Retrospective Adoption Cohorts, Composition versus Place, and the Role of Aging and Labor Shortages
26e942feef:6ade09d9ef1d30fe.author: Takahiro Tabuchi
26e942feef:6ade09d9ef1d30fe.summary: Japan has the lowest rate of generative AI use among major economies, yet little is known about how the technology has spread within the country. This study uses the sixth wave of the Japan COVID-19 and Society Internet Survey (JACSIS, N = 27, 630), which asks respondents when they first started using generative AI, to reconstruct cumulative adoption curves for Japanese municipalities from November 2022 to January 2026. Because every respondent became able to adopt at the same moment, the release of ChatGPT, the retrospective cohorts support a discrete-time hazard analysis without left truncation. Linking postal codes to municipal statistics, we document four findings. First, adoption follows the urban hierarchy: by January 2026, 50% of residents of the quintile of municipalities with the highest population density had adopted, compared with 35% in the quintile with the lowest population density, and the ratio between the two rose from 0.55 to 0.71 over the four periods, indicating relative convergence alongside a widening absolute gap. Second, most of the geographic gradient reflects who lives where rather than where they live: individual characteristics explain 64% of the population-density coefficient, and the coefficients on population density and on distance to Tokyo become statistically indistinguishable from zero once individual controls are included. Third, municipal population aging is negatively associated with adoption beyond its compositional effect, but only in the first two years of diffusion. Fourth, the job openings-to-applicants ratio in the respondent's workplace area is positively associated with work-related adoption and unrelated to purely private adoption, a pattern consistent with labor scarcity pulling generative AI into workplaces. The association is statistically significant but economically small: a one-point increase in the ratio is associated with a work-adoption probability less than one percentage point higher. 26e942feef:0f96c39b65f1fad9.title: Emissions-adjusted total factor productivity
26e942feef:0f96c39b65f1fad9.author: Rachel, Lukasz
26e942feef:0f96c39b65f1fad9.summary: In many economies, the recent productivity slowdown coincided with declines in carbon dioxide emissions. Productivity statistics ignore this progress, even though lower emissions raise future consumption. We propose emissions-adjusted total factor productivity (TFPE), a forward-looking, welfare-relevant productivity measure. TFPE requires few assumptions, relying on the social cost of carbon as a sufficient statistic. At recent consensus estimates of the social cost of carbon, U.S. TFPE could grow twice as fast as TFP during a transition to net zero by 2050. At these costs of carbon, historical productivity adjustments are modest; at higher values, the post-2005 U.S. productivity slowdown disappears. In other countries, TFPE growth significantly exceeds TFP growth during the 1990s.

26e942feef:7dc29b3ed1f2481b.title: Scientific isolation? The consequences of Trump's China initiative on Chinese research
26e942feef:7dc29b3ed1f2481b.author: Westin, Karolina
26e942feef:7dc29b3ed1f2481b.summary: The 2018 China Initiative by the Trump administration complicated procedures and reduced funding for U.S.-China research collaborations. Using Scopus data, we analyze its impact on Chinese research. We find that it significantly lowered the quality of both publications and co-authors of Chinese researchers with prior U.S. collaborations compared to those with prior European collaborations, and reduced yearly citations for affected researchers by 6%. The effect was stronger for high-productivity Chinese researchers in U.S.-dominated fields. While China is at the forefront of the scientific frontier, it still depends more on the U.S. than the reverse.
