901dc0be66:726c580558eff521.title: How New Products Enter Markets: Social Networks, Consumer Imports, and Retailer Learning*
901dc0be66:726c580558eff521.summary: Abstract This paper studies how new varieties enter markets and become locally available. We provide causal evidence of demand externalities that operate in two steps. First, information about new varieties diffuses directly through real-world social ties among consumers. Second, early purchases generate an indirect spillover to firms: local retailers learn from “pioneer” consumers which new varieties are most likely to succeed and adjust their product offerings accordingly. We study this process in the context of direct-to-consumer imports. Using customs records on individuals ’ purchases matched to population-wide social networks, international migrant links, and retailer catchment areas, we document economically meaningful demand externalities. Product-specific expenditure shocks abroad transmit through migrant networks and shift which varieties consumers purchase. Leveraging these shocks as a plausibly exogenous source of local demand variation, we show strong peer effects: prior purchases by close neighbors, coworkers, or friends increase an individual’s likelihood of purchasing the same variety, especially for premium and visible goods. We leverage this result to identify an indirect spillover from consumers to firms: retailers are more likely to add a variety to their assortment when it becomes popular among consumers in their catchment area. Combining the instrument with linked consumer–retailer data and a self-conducted retailer survey, we show that this response reflects learning about latent demand for varieties not yet stocked locally. Together, social diffusion and retailer learning generate demand multipliers that reshape local product availability and expand access to global variety.

901dc0be66:a03b417b94c31fd5.title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk, and Moral Hazard*
901dc0be66:a03b417b94c31fd5.summary: Abstract Intensifying climate change makes protection against natural disaster risk – either through ex ante insurance or ex post aid – a first-order public policy issue. Flood risk protection in the U.S. traditionally featured ex post aid through FEMA and heavily subsidized insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). In an effort to correct subsidy-induced overbuilding and under-mitigation in flood-prone areas, the NFIP recently moved to actuarially fair insurance premiums. But this change has two unintended consequences: a fiscal spillover onto FEMA disaster aid as insurance coverage declines in flood-prone areas, and household exposure to uninsurable reclassification risk from uncertain climate projections. We develop a model of optimal flood insurance that incorporates the static and dynamic tradeoffs of subsidizing premiums. We then use a variety of identification strategies and data to estimate the five key parameters needed to implement this model. We find that the fiscal spillover and reclassification risk protection benefits significantly outweigh the moral hazard costs, and that the optimal subsidy to flood insurance is 51%, comparable to the level of subsidization before the recent reform.

901dc0be66:62a3a5dec33f1007.title: Retrieval Failures and Consumption Smoothing: A Field Experiment on Seasonal Poverty*
901dc0be66:62a3a5dec33f1007.summary: Abstract People may fail to recall and use information they already know when making decisions. We empirically investigate whether such “retrieval failures” distort consumption-smoothing behavior among Zambian farmers, who derive their income from one annual harvest and spend it over the course of the year. We document that individuals underestimate upcoming spending by 50%, creating scope for undersaving. To improve recall, we randomize an intervention that prompts people to think through their future expenses associatively in categories—without providing any external information or guidance. Treated individuals increase “remembered” expenses by 36%–60%; as predicted by the memory literature, effects are concentrated among small, irregular, and stochastic items. Immediate spending drops and, six weeks after the intervention, treated households hold 15% higher savings. They subsequently enter the hungry season—the final months of the year when consumption typically declines sharply—with one additional month of savings, leading to a flatter spending profile over the year. Households use the increased savings to self-finance additional farm investment, resulting in a 9% increase in the next year’s crop revenue. We replicate the intervention’s effect on beliefs among low-income Americans, suggesting that retrieval failures generalize across settings and populations.

901dc0be66:b3e6cc3c7ea671f4.title: The Origin of Risk*
901dc0be66:b3e6cc3c7ea671f4.summary: Abstract We propose a tractable model in which risk, at both the micro and macro levels, is endogenous and driven by incentives. In the model, each firm chooses the mean and the variance of its productivity process, as well as how it covaries with the productivity of other firms. Aggregate risk arises when firms select productivity processes that are correlated with one another. The theory predicts that larger firms and those with lower markups are less volatile and less correlated with aggregate productivity. We find support for these predictions in the data. Through their impact on risk-taking decisions, distortions such as taxes and markups can make GDP more volatile in equilibrium. In a calibrated version of the model, removing distortions significantly reduces GDP volatility.

901dc0be66:c79bdfba8535da03.title: Busing to Opportunity? The Impacts of the METCO Voluntary School Desegregation Program on Urban Students of Color
901dc0be66:c79bdfba8535da03.summary: Abstract School assignment policies are a key lever for expanding access to high-performing schools and promoting racial and socioeconomic integration. For over 50 years, the Metropolitan Council for Educational Opportunity (METCO) has bussed students of color from Boston, Massachusetts to relatively wealthier and predominantly White suburbs. I estimate the effects of attending a high-performing suburban school by comparing applicants who receive enrollment offers with applicants who do not. A two-stage least squares approach exploits waitlist assignment priorities and controls for a rich set of characteristics from birth records and application data. Attending a suburban school boosts math and English test scores, reduces dropout, and increases on-time high school graduation. Four-year college aspirations, enrollment, and graduation increase along with earnings in adulthood. Students whose parents did not attend college and boys experience the largest effects. The evidence points to several mechanisms, including access to higher value-added schools, higher achieving peers, and schools with stronger college-going norms. Participants are more likely to be tracked into lower performing classes, implying that effects could be larger with access to more advanced coursework. District value-added estimates suggest that students’ educational trajectories shift at least as much as they would from growing up in the suburban districts.

901dc0be66:d764e9a33aa9f165.title: How Does Wage Inequality Affect the Labor Movement?*
901dc0be66:d764e9a33aa9f165.summary: Abstract This paper provides evidence on how wage inequality among workers affects the labor movement using three complementary research designs: a vignette experiment with union organizers, a natural policy experiment that increased wage inequality among Wisconsin school teachers, and an information intervention during the 2023 Writers Guild of America strike. Across all studies, we find that inequality undermines union strength through multiple channels. First, workers with high individual bargaining power are more likely to withdraw support in unequal environments, preferring individual over collective bargaining. Second, union organizers facing hypothetical choices strategically respond to inequality in ways that may preserve membership but limit redistribution, such as shifting their campaign away from wages and choosing smaller, more homogeneous bargaining units.

901dc0be66:7e3356847366fb7c.title: Bringing Work Home: Flexible Work Arrangements as Gateway Jobs for Women in West Bengal*
901dc0be66:7e3356847366fb7c.summary: Abstract There is a large latent workforce in developing countries that consists of hundreds of millions of women who prefer to have paid work and yet are out of the labor force. Often, available job opportunities are incompatible with traditional gender roles that encourage women to stay at home. In a randomized experiment with 1,670 households, we partner with a jobs platform to offer short-term data work to women who are out of the labor force. We find three main results. First, flexible work-from-home jobs are highly effective at bringing women into paid work. Job flexibility more than triples take-up from 15% for an office job to 48% for a job that women can do from home while multitasking with childcare. Second, these jobs can act as a stepping stone to less flexible work. Trying paid work from home increases take-up of less flexible jobs two to three months later among women without previous work experience. “Gateway jobs” are especially important for women from more traditional households: their labor supply is more likely to be marginal to flexibility, and in turn, work experience shifts their attitudes to become less traditional. Third, from the labor demand side, remote work comes with trade-offs in worker performance. Working from the office increases accuracy by 3% and speed by 18%. However, these performance drawbacks of work-from-home arrangements may be outweighed by the increase in available workers.

901dc0be66:cd8a21a11e8e6cb5.title: Attention to the Macroeconomy*
901dc0be66:cd8a21a11e8e6cb5.summary: Abstract We measure which economic topics are top of mind using quarterly German household and firm panels from 2020 to 2024, a period that spans the post-pandemic inflation surge and the subsequent disinflation. With these data, we study potential determinants and consequences of having inflation top of mind. In line with goal-directed attention, the likelihood that inflation is top of mind rises with proxies for its true payoff relevance. At the same time, prior experiences predict whether respondents have inflation and energy prices top of mind conditional on a large set of controls for payoff relevance, and this relationship strengthens when the environment becomes more inflationary. Having inflation top of mind predicts stronger increases in information acquisition and inflation expectations over the shock period. At odds with goal-optimality, having inflation top of mind is associated with expectations further away from multiple ex-ante benchmarks. Finally, both key determinants of having inflation top of mind—payoff relevance and prior experiences—are associated with stronger shifts of expectations away from these benchmarks over the shock period.

Lowry’s factories, streets, and soccer matches, paying tribute to the great chronicler of England’s interwar working-class culture By Andrew Pulver It is appropriate that a new exhibition of works by L. S. Lowry (1887–1976), opening today at the MK Gallery, should be staged in Milton Keynes. Established after the Second World War, it is the largest of the “new towns” that were built to accommodate the huge numbers of British working people displaced by enemy bombing, slum clearance, and industrial decline. Lowry’s most notable paintings are both a celebration of and a tribute to the working-class culture of the interwar period—and they passed into mainstream ubiquity in the 1940s and 1950s just as that culture was collapsing. Fifty-four miles north of London, and 160 miles south of Lowry’s base of operations in Manchester, Milton Keynes is arguably the most consequential monument to England’s postwar upheaval. READ ON

f965d2251a:62a3a5dec33f1007.title: Retrieval Failures and Consumption Smoothing: A Field Experiment on Seasonal Poverty*
f965d2251a:62a3a5dec33f1007.summary: Abstract People may fail to recall and use information they already know when making decisions. We empirically investigate whether such “retrieval failures” distort consumption-smoothing behavior among Zambian farmers, who derive their income from one annual harvest and spend it over the course of the year. We document that individuals underestimate upcoming spending by 50%, creating scope for undersaving. To improve recall, we randomize an intervention that prompts people to think through their future expenses associatively in categories—without providing any external information or guidance. Treated individuals increase “remembered” expenses by 36%–60%; as predicted by the memory literature, effects are concentrated among small, irregular, and stochastic items. Immediate spending drops and, six weeks after the intervention, treated households hold 15% higher savings. They subsequently enter the hungry season—the final months of the year when consumption typically declines sharply—with one additional month of savings, leading to a flatter spending profile over the year. Households use the increased savings to self-finance additional farm investment, resulting in a 9% increase in the next year’s crop revenue. We replicate the intervention’s effect on beliefs among low-income Americans, suggesting that retrieval failures generalize across settings and populations.

f965d2251a:c79bdfba8535da03.title: Busing to Opportunity? The Impacts of the Metco Voluntary School Desegregation Program on Urban Students of Color
f965d2251a:c79bdfba8535da03.summary: Abstract School assignment policies are a key lever for expanding access to high-performing schools and promoting racial and socioeconomic integration. For over 50 years, the Metropolitan Council for Educational Opportunity (METCO) has bussed students of color from Boston, Massachusetts, to relatively wealthier and predominantly white suburbs. I estimate the effects of attending a high-performing suburban school by comparing applicants who receive enrollment offers with applicants who do not. A two-stage least squares approach exploits waitlist assignment priorities and controls for a rich set of characteristics from birth records and application data. Attending a suburban school boosts math and English test scores, reduces dropout, and increases on-time high school graduation. Four-year college aspirations, enrollment, and graduation increase along with earnings in adulthood. Students whose parents did not attend college and boys experience the largest effects. The evidence points to several mechanisms, including access to higher value-added schools, higher-achieving peers, and schools with stronger college-going norms. Participants are more likely to be tracked into lower-performing classes, implying that effects could be larger with access to more advanced coursework. District value-added estimates suggest that students’ educational trajectories shift at least as much as they would from growing up in the suburban districts.

f965d2251a:7e3356847366fb7c.title: Bringing Work Home: Flexible Work Arrangements as Gateway Jobs for Women in West Bengal*
f965d2251a:7e3356847366fb7c.summary: Abstract There is a large latent workforce in developing countries that consists of hundreds of millions of women who prefer to have paid work and yet are out of the labor force. Often, available job opportunities are incompatible with traditional gender roles that encourage women to stay at home. In a randomized experiment with 1,670 households, we partner with a jobs platform to offer short-term data work to women who are out of the labor force. We find three main results. First, flexible work-from-home jobs are highly effective at bringing women into paid work. Job flexibility more than triples take-up from 15% for an office job to 48% for a job that women can do from home while multitasking with childcare. Second, these jobs can act as a stepping stone to less flexible work. Trying paid work from home increases take-up of less flexible jobs two to three months later among women without previous work experience. “Gateway jobs” are especially important for women from more traditional households: their labor supply is more likely to be marginal to flexibility, and in turn, work experience shifts their attitudes to become less traditional. Third, from the labor demand side, remote work comes with trade-offs in worker performance. Working from the office increases accuracy by 3% and speed by 18%. However, these performance drawbacks of work-from-home arrangements may be outweighed by the increase in available workers.

f965d2251a:e4c5cce8c2a59ace.title: Fairness Across the World
f965d2251a:e4c5cce8c2a59ace.summary: Abstract This article provides the first comprehensive global evidence on people’s fairness and efficiency preferences, beliefs about the sources of inequality and the efficiency cost of redistribution, and policy attitudes toward redistribution. Using a globally harmonized consequential experiment with more than 65,000 individuals across 60 countries, we show that the source of inequality plays a substantially larger role for inequality acceptance than the efficiency cost of redistribution. At the global level, implemented inequality increases by 85% when inequality is caused by merit rather than luck, compared with a 14% increase when redistribution entails a 50% efficiency cost. We document substantial heterogeneity in fairness views and beliefs within and across societies. The meritocratic fairness view is most prominent in many richer Western societies, while libertarian and egalitarian fairness views are widespread in many other parts of the world. Globally, people are more likely to believe that inequality reflects luck rather than merit, while beliefs in large efficiency costs of redistribution are relatively weak. Fairness preferences and beliefs are strongly associated with redistribution attitudes and actual redistribution through taxes and transfers across countries. Our findings illustrate how the interaction between fairness views and beliefs may shape redistribution across societies, highlighting the importance of jointly understanding preferences and beliefs in the political economy of redistribution.

f965d2251a:c5028e4bcde9f322.title: Wealth and Property Taxation in the United States*
f965d2251a:c5028e4bcde9f322.summary: Abstract We study the history and geography of wealth accumulation in the United States using newly collected historical property tax records from the early 1800s onward. These records come from the administration of the General Property Tax—a tax that aspired to cover all types of property. We construct wealth series at the state, county, and national levels. At the state level, we use annual assessed values of wealth from state-level reports drawn from multiple sources. Because assessed values may differ from market values, we also require assessment ratios, defined as the ratio of assessed to market wealth. We obtain state-level assessment ratios from decadal U.S. Census wealth data (drawn from various census reports, including those on “Wealth, Debt, and Taxation”), in which the census carried out detailed valuation work, complemented with information on changes in assessment practices from the state reports, to build higher-frequency series of assessment ratios. The result is long-run annual wealth series for states from 1850 (or earlier, depending on the state) to 1935. We obtain national wealth series by aggregating these state series. At the county level, we use assessed values (or market values where available) from the U.S. Census wealth data for each decade and apply either state-level or county-level assessment ratios, where available, to obtain market values of wealth for each decade from 1850 to 1930. We use these data to show, first, that the United States experienced extraordinary wealth accumulation after the Civil War and until the Great Depression. Second, spatial inequality in the United States has been large and highly persistent since the mid-1800s. We also examine the determinants of long-term wealth growth and find, among other results, that counties with a higher share of enslaved property before the Civil War or with higher wealth inequality experienced lower subsequent long-run wealth growth.

56c7f0b50e:22573729eeba6cf3.title: Why Don't Jobseekers Search More ? Barriers and Returns to Search on a Job
56c7f0b50e:22573729eeba6cf3.author: Field, Erica
56c7f0b50e:22573729eeba6cf3.summary: Understanding specific barriers to job search and returns to relaxing these barriers is important for economists and policymakers. An experiment that changed the default process for initiating job applications increased applications by 600 percent on a search platform in Pakistan. Perhaps surprisingly, the marginal treatment-induced applications have approximately constant rather than decreasing returns. These results are consistent with a directed search model in which some jobseekers miss some high-return vacancies due to the psychological costs of initiating applications. These findings show that small reductions in search costs can substantially improve search outcomes in environments with some relatively inactive jobseekers.

56c7f0b50e:f5defd7842cc1ab9.title: Vacancy referrals and broader job search: the role of spillovers among caseworkers
56c7f0b50e:f5defd7842cc1ab9.author: Hossain, Mohammad Zariab
56c7f0b50e:f5defd7842cc1ab9.summary: This paper provides the first causal evidence of behavioral spillovers in public employment services (PES). Using rich Swedish administrative data from 2004–2018 and a difference-in-differences design exploiting caseworker moves across local PES offices, I show that caseworker’s broader vacancy referral behavior—vacancy referrals outside a job seeker’s stated preferences—responds strongly to the local work-practice styles. I also examine how these practice-environment shocks of the movers (caseworkers) affect their job seekers. Taken together, the evidence suggests that local referral practices and the surrounding organizational environment play an important role in shaping caseworker behavior, with consequences for job seekers’ reemployment prospects.

56c7f0b50e:1fbb7ea2d7e4dbbe.title: Peers and careers: unequal returns to elite alumni networks
56c7f0b50e:1fbb7ea2d7e4dbbe.author: Walldorf, Jeanette
56c7f0b50e:1fbb7ea2d7e4dbbe.summary: Do alumni ties preserve economic advantage? Linking random tutorial-group assignments at a Danish business school to administrative career data, we show that students align careers more with group peers than others in the same cohort, particularly through shared workplaces. These effects are especially pronounced among students from the wealthiest families and concentrated in top-paying firms. More exposure to affluent peers raises earnings, access to top-paying jobs, and increases the probability of reaching the top income ranks for similarly privileged students, while not for others. Job transitions to group peers point to gains from peer-connected moves, again concentrated among wealthier students.

56c7f0b50e:a010f9f8a7082500.title: Relaxing Immigration Restrictions in a Peripheral Region: Evidence from Finnish North Karelia
56c7f0b50e:a010f9f8a7082500.author: Jeremias Nieminen
56c7f0b50e:a010f9f8a7082500.summary: Several countries use immigration liberalization as a place-based policy tool, but evidence on its regional effects remains almost entirely descriptive. We examine the causal impact of removing labor market testing (LMT) regulations for labor immigrants in all occupations in the remote Finnish region of North Karelia. The reform allowed firms to hire non-EU foreign workers in all occupations without first advertising jobs to domestic applicants, resulting in a 14% rise in the stock of immigrant workers. Using synthetic control and difference-in-differences methods, we estimate causal effects of the reform at the regional, municipal, firm establishment, and individual levels. The reform caused immigrant inflows to increase primarily in cities and in specific types of occupations, i.e., low-paying occupations and ISCO groups 5, 7, 8, and 9. Across the firm size distribution, the increases concentrate around the median and the top. We find little evidence that the policy had meaningful effects on other regional or municipal outcomes: immigration liberalization boosted labor supply without generating transformative medium-term regional effects.

56c7f0b50e:10f2fee9e48dd8d1.title: Competing for workers: labor market transmission of firm export
56c7f0b50e:10f2fee9e48dd8d1.author: Gorshkov, Andrei
56c7f0b50e:10f2fee9e48dd8d1.summary: We study the transmission of firm-specific export shocks through labor markets, examining how these shocks influence workers’ wages at competing firms via labor market competition. Using rich Danish administrative data, a flexible, empirically driven definition of workers’ outside options, and an identification strategy based on world import demand shocks, we show that both own-firm and competitor export shocks raise incumbent workers’ wages. These export-driven shocks also trigger competitive worker reallocation, as expanding exporters poach workers from other firms. The results indicate spillover effects of export shocks extending to non-exporting firms.

0cf31f7a1a:fb60adac70e2fd09.title: Can Civic Mobilization Reduce Sexual Violence? Evidence from March 4 Justice Demonstrations in Australia
0cf31f7a1a:fb60adac70e2fd09.author: Astghik Mavisakalyan
0cf31f7a1a:fb60adac70e2fd09.summary: Civic mobilization is a common societal response to gender-based violence, but whether it actually changes sexual offending is largely unknown. We exploit geographic variation in exposure to the March 4 Justice (M4J) movement — a nationally coordinated series of protests against gender-based violence held across Australia on 15th March 2021 — as a natural experiment, using a difference-in-differences design. We find that areas hosting the protests experienced a 16 to 21 per cent reduction in recorded sexual assaults over the six to twelve months following the movement, with no significant effects across six other crime categories. This suggests a mechanism specific to sexual violence rather than general deterrence. These effects are larger in locations closer to protest activity and at sites with sizable crowds compared to smaller ones. Attitudinal data from the National Community Attitudes towards Violence against Women Survey reveal significant shifts in men’s attitudes: greater rejection of rape myths, increased survivor credibility, and reduced endorsement of patriarchal norms, with these shifts concentrated among younger and more educated men. The reductions in sexual assault are concentrated in male-represented areas, where the movement’s normative signal was more novel, and nationwide, we find suggestive evidence of a modest rise in female electoral support in 2022 relative to 2019. Together, these findings suggest that civic mobilization can reduce violence through the internalization of norms.

0cf31f7a1a:6d3606d9900690c5.title: Closure without Resolution in European Prison Oversight
0cf31f7a1a:6d3606d9900690c5.author: Ismail, Nasrul
0cf31f7a1a:6d3606d9900690c5.summary: Compliance with judgments of the European Court of Human Rights is conventionally recorded as a terminal status: a case is open or closed, a judgment executed or pending, an obligation met or unmet. These measures enable scholarly comparison, but they cannot show how a state engages with the supervision of a judgment or whether reform of prison conditions endures. As such, this article treats compliance as conduct and asks whether the closure of supervision reflects durable improvement in the conditions a judgment addressed. Drawing on the documentary record of Committee of Ministers supervision in three pilot-judgment jurisdictions (i.e., Italy, Romania, and Hungary), with two contextual comparators (i.e., Spain and England and Wales), it codes state disclosures for opacity and stance and reconstructs responsiveness descriptively from the dated supervisory sequence. Two independent coders reached strong agreement (Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.88 for stance and 0.90 for opacity, on small, well-specified eligible data sets). The cases did not form a single compliance scale but displayed distinct configurations. Specifically, Italy was transparent but shifted in its stated position before closure in 2016; Romania combined continuing engagement with capacity explanations; and Hungary combined formal but insubstantial engagement with selective disclosure. Set against current prison occupancy, the state that had completed supervision was the most overcrowded: Italy recorded 120.7 occupants per 100 places, exceeding Hungary's 114.5 and Romania's 111.2. Because the occupancy snapshot postdated Italy's closure, it could not reveal whether closure caused the later overcrowding, but it did manifest that closure did not secure lasting improvement in reforms. The article frames this durability gap as a problem of means-ends decoupling and offers a reproducible method for distinguishing compliance conduct from the substantive conditions oversight exists to change.

0cf31f7a1a:6570357cd13a1007.title: Optimal Line-Drawing for Legal Rules
0cf31f7a1a:6570357cd13a1007.author: David Weisbach
0cf31f7a1a:6570357cd13a1007.summary: Line drawing is a pervasive feature of legal systems. Across many domains, the applicable legal treatment turns on whether an activity falls above or below some threshold. We characterize the economic forces that determine the optimal placement of such thresholds, both generally and in specific legal settings involving monetary and non-monetary sanctions, prohibitions, and mandates. We apply our results to two important line-drawing questions in private law: the optimal due-care threshold for negligence liability and the optimal threshold for whether a shortfall in contract performance constitutes breach. In both applications, the optimal line takes the form of a population-level marginal cost-benefit rule, with the relevant costs and benefits weighted over the actors whose behavior the line induces to change.

0cf31f7a1a:e11f6205fdc6191f.title: The Regulatory Burden of Licensure Sales Laws: New Evidence on Race and the U.S. Tobacco Market
0cf31f7a1a:e11f6205fdc6191f.author: Joseph J. Sabia
0cf31f7a1a:e11f6205fdc6191f.summary: Licensure sales requirements are commonly justified as consumer protection regulations intended to improve seller compliance and reduce harm associated with risky products. However, licensure effects may differ across communities with heterogeneous enforcement intensity and seller responses. We study this question in the context of e-cigarette retail licensure laws (ERLLs), a policy intended to regulate access to e-cigarettes among youth. We find that state ERLLs with strong penalties for non-compliance reduce nicotine vaping among Black youths by 2.5-4.0 percentage points but have no effect on White youths. This racially disparate finding is driven by heterogeneous supply-side responses to increased regulatory burden. Vendors in Black neighborhoods are more likely to be targeted for inspections than those in White neighborhoods despite having lower pre-treatment rates of infractions. Moreover, vendors in Black neighborhoods are also less likely to sell e-cigarettes following ERLL adoption, consistent with a racially disparate regulatory burden. Together, our results suggest important distributional consequences of licensure requirements.

0cf31f7a1a:ce8cde7506173463.title: Who Replaces Spirit? Entry, Exit, and Low-End Fares
0cf31f7a1a:ce8cde7506173463.author: E. Mina Guler
0cf31f7a1a:ce8cde7506173463.summary: A federal court blocked JetBlue’s acquisition of Spirit Airlines in January 2024 to protect consumers who relied on Spirit’s low fares. Spirit failed anyway and ceased operations in May 2026. We ask whether the prohibition protected consumers. Using DB1B data for 2022–2025, we estimate the effect of Spirit’s exit across the 1, 427 routes it served. The 5th and 10th percentile fares rise by 8.6 and 5.8 log points; mean and median fares are unaffected. Where a carrier entered, the bottom is unaffected and mean fares fall. Theharm comes from exit without replacement, which entry policy does not reach.

0cf31f7a1a:ab73add37d884e06.title: A Path-Dependent Agent-Based Microsimulation of Crime and Violence Reduction Policy Portfolios in Bolivia: Survey Calibration, Adaptive Emulator Ensembles, Global Sensitivity, Tempered MCMC, and Multi-Objective Policy Analysis
0cf31f7a1a:ab73add37d884e06.author: Ricardo Alonzo Fern\'andez-Salguero
0cf31f7a1a:ab73add37d884e06.summary: This study develops a survey-calibrated, path-dependent agent-based microsimulation for evaluating crime and violence reduction policies in Bolivia. A synthetic population is constructed from the 2025 Household Survey and the fourth-quarter 2025 Continuous Employment Survey using official expansion weights and cross-survey donor matching. The model combines heterogeneous agents, place-based risk, criminal adaptation, institutional capacity, community organization, and multiple policy channels. Uncertainty is propagated through adaptive Gaussian-process and tree-ensemble emulators, global sensitivity analysis, tempered ensemble MCMC, and predictive meta-calibration. Simulated portfolios include focused policing, community control, Guardabosques-type incentives, social prevention, environmental interventions, justice reforms, investigation, rehabilitation, and financial-network disruption. Results are interpreted as structural policy scenarios rather than causal forecasts, with explicit attention to displacement, distributional effects, implementation capacity, and multi-objective trade-offs.

0cf31f7a1a:82aed7fba070816d.title: Aligning Platform and User Incentives in Social Media Age Restrictions
0cf31f7a1a:82aed7fba070816d.author: Christopher Roth
0cf31f7a1a:82aed7fba070816d.summary: Several countries are adopting social media bans for teenagers, yet early evidence suggests limited adherence to the age-based restrictions. Such bans ask platforms to remove profitable customers and teens to give up access to their online social networks. We study an alternative regulatory regime in which platforms remain liable for teens on the adult tier but may offer a safe tier that removes restricted features, such as algorithmic feeds, while preserving interactions with their relevant network. Provision of the safe tier and enforcement are complementary: teens can adhere without giving up access to their network, and platforms can retain displaced adult-tier users as lower-margin customers. This policy design makes the teen decision to avoid the adult tier less dependent on peer dynamics and increases teen welfare for a relevant range of regulatory penalties.

0cf31f7a1a:544ac7a5d8c9314e.title: Put Your Money Where Your Mouth Is: Defending Commercial Reasonableness in Insurance Law's Duty to Make Reasonable Settlement Decisions
0cf31f7a1a:544ac7a5d8c9314e.author: Melikian, Sarah
0cf31f7a1a:544ac7a5d8c9314e.summary: This Comment examines the Restatement of the Law, Liability Insurance’s adoption of an objective commercial reasonableness standard for an insurer’s duty to make reasonable settlement decisions and argues that the standard appropriately balances the interests of insurers and policyholders. After reviewing the origins of liability insurance, the insurer’s duties to defend and indemnify, and the development of the duty to settle, the Comment analyzes the controversy surrounding the American Law Institute’s Restatement project and the criticism directed at its treatment of settlement obligations. The Comment contends that a commercial reasonableness standard is necessary because insurers possess exclusive control over settlement decisions and may otherwise be incentivized to expose policyholders to excess judgments while risking only policy-limit liability. By requiring insurers to evaluate settlement opportunities as though they alone would bear the full financial consequences of an adverse judgment, the Restatement aligns insurer incentives with the interests of insureds and promotes fair decision-making. The Comment further argues that concerns about excessive insurer liability are overstated, as courts applying objective reasonableness standards continue to uphold insurer decisions when settlement demands are unreasonable. Ultimately, the Comment concludes that the Restatement’s approach both clarifies a historically confusing area of insurance law and provides a sound framework for protecting policyholders without unfairly burdening insurers. [This abstract was written by Microsoft Copilot, a generative artificial intelligence.]

0cf31f7a1a:aac47bf92846dad2.title: From prison peers to co-offenders
0cf31f7a1a:aac47bf92846dad2.author: Laura Khoury
0cf31f7a1a:aac47bf92846dad2.summary: This paper provides direct evidence that shared incarceration can facilitate the formation of post-release criminal partnerships. Using Norwegian administrative data linking prison spells to police case identifiers, we measure network ties through subsequent co-offending. We exploit time-based variation in exposure within facilities by comparing inmate pairs in the same facility who differ only in whether their spells overlapped. Overlap is associated with a 37% increase in five-year co-offending relative to comparable non-overlapping pairs, robust to extensive controls and timing-based restrictions. Effects are stronger in environments and for pairs where interaction is plausibly more intense, highlighting network formation as a plausible mechanism.

0cf31f7a1a:94a352f35b52fdd0.title: Competition law enforcement in informal markets in Latin America and the Caribbean
0cf31f7a1a:94a352f35b52fdd0.author: OECD
0cf31f7a1a:94a352f35b52fdd0.summary: This paper examines the challenges faced by competition authorities in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) when enforcing competition law in markets affected by informality. Informal markets represent a significant share of economic activity in the region and may influence competitive dynamics both where informal firms compete with formal firms and where competition occurs within informal markets. The paper focusses on competition enforcement issues related to informality including the definition of relevant markets, the investigation of informal firms and the calculation of fines. Although informality can create substantial evidentiary and procedural difficulties, the paper identifies opportunities for competition authorities to mitigate those challenges, including the use of official datasets, market studies and institutional co-operation with organisations addressing informality. The paper argues that competition authorities in LAC should be mindful of informal markets when enforcing competition law, and can apply proportionate, pragmatic and targeted enforcement to address competitive harm involving informal markets, while supporting better market functioning and the transition towards formality.

0cf31f7a1a:f3b90c5f5e94869c.title: Early resolution of cartel cases in Latin America and the Caribbean
0cf31f7a1a:f3b90c5f5e94869c.author: OECD
0cf31f7a1a:f3b90c5f5e94869c.summary: This paper provides an overview of the state of play of early resolution of cartel cases in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) jurisdictions, covering the legal framework, enforcement experiences, as well as challenges and particularities. Competition authorities may benefit from the early resolution of cartel cases by saving on time and the resources that the case would require in an adversarial procedure, allocating them more efficiently to the detection and prosecution of other cartels and providing for a greater deterrence and wider impact of their enforcement actions. The paper highlights that LAC competition authorities may consider designing and using these tools as a way to achieve procedural expediency. The design and implementation of early resolution programmes requires consideration of the incentives of parties to resolve cases early and the interplay with leniency programmes, damages and the pursuit of other policy objectives.

0cf31f7a1a:fe294172792f6e83.title: Automated Suspicion: Algorithmic Workforce Surveillance and the Erosion of Internal Legitimacy in the Metropolitan Police Service
0cf31f7a1a:fe294172792f6e83.author: Ford, Paul
0cf31f7a1a:fe294172792f6e83.summary: Abstract This article examines the Metropolitan Police Service (MPS) pilot deployment of Palantir analytics for internal workforce monitoring, announced in April 2026 as part of the force’s post-Panorama standards programme. The force defends the deployment as lawful, since it brings together data it already holds; this article argues that defence repeats a known mistake in policing legitimacy research, treating legal compliance as the ceiling of consent rather than its floor. Drawing on procedural justice theory (Tyler 2006), the dialogic and twin-track models of legitimacy (Bottoms and Tankebe 2012; Tankebe 2013; Bradford and Tankebe 2014), Beetham’s (1991) account of institutional legitimacy, and the author’s earlier work (Ford 2021, 2026), it audits the deployment against the four pillars of procedural justice and finds it deficient on voice, neutrality, respect, and trustworthy motives. It argues that the pilot inverts Sherman’s (2007) power-few hypothesis, fails the targeting—testing—tracking discipline of evidence-based policing (Sherman 2013), substitutes a technical fix for what Heifetz (1994) calls an adaptive challenge, and entangles culture reform with surveillance in ways that risk delegitimising Equality, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI) work and, through a mirroring effect, damaging public-facing encounters. A subsequent disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, including the pilot’s Data Protection Impact Assessment and Equality Impact Assessment obtained in redacted form, tests these claims against primary evidence: it confirms an algorithmic yield of 2.6 million flags with a further-action rate of 0.075 per cent, corroborates self-acknowledged risks to trust and equity in the MPS’s own equalities analysis, and shows the force cannot establish what became of the cases its own system flagged. The article closes with implications for chief officers, police and crime commissioners, and professional standards leads. Keywords: algorithmic…

0cf31f7a1a:f1948c91d38cbf2b.title: Beyond the Dark Figure: A Causal and Probabilistic Analysis of Crimes Against Women in India
0cf31f7a1a:f1948c91d38cbf2b.author: Ghosh, Rudrani
0cf31f7a1a:f1948c91d38cbf2b.summary: Most research on violence against women in India depends on administrative police records. However, this raw data often suffers from severe reporting biases and fails to account for massive population differences between districts. To address these flaws, this study applies causal inference, hierarchical modeling, and machine learning to better understand local crime dynamics. By combining two decades of National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) statistics with 2011 Census demographics, we map both the spatial distribution and the true sociological drivers of this violence. We found no evidence of geographic clustering; a Moran's I analysis shows the violence is distributed randomly across the country. Furthermore, our mixed-effects hierarchical models indicate that broad state-level policies explain less than 1% of the variance in local crime rates. Furthermore, by applying Pearl's do-calculus and Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), we isolate the causal effects of the male-female literacy gap and urbanization, proving that urbanization is the dominant driver of reporting rates. A Bayesian Structural Time Series (BSTS) correctly isolates the passage of the 2013 Criminal Law (Amendment) Act as an administrative reporting shock yielding an 88, 879 annual case surge rather than a behavioral epidemic. Finally, Bayesian Belief Networks are utilized to model highly nonlinear sociological interactions, providing a mathematical framework for proactive risk assessment.

Department of Corrections (D.C. DOC) correctional facilities. The Justice Department will investigate whether D.C. DOC engages in a pattern or practice of violating prisoners’ and detainees’ constitutional rights.

daedf173a6:ff7e9c6fe0542830.title: Justice Department Announces Settlement Ending Antisemitism and Race Discrimination at UNC
daedf173a6:ff7e9c6fe0542830.summary: This week the U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division and the U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights (ED-OCR) entered a voluntary university-wide settlement agreement with the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC) to end antisemitism and race discrimination. daedf173a6:5342a836764c3818.summary: Today, the Justice Department announced charges involving 16 aliens in North Carolina, New York, and Idaho, including an illegal alien, in connection with illegal voting, false claims of U.S. citizenship, and related election crimes. The cases include voting by aliens in federal elections and false claims of U.S. citizenship to register to vote or to vote.

daedf173a6:1916c37e2900c593.title: Somerset Lifesciences Inc. Agrees to Pay $4M to Resolve Allegations of Causing Medicare to Pay Claims for its Mislabeled Generic Drug
daedf173a6:1916c37e2900c593.summary: Somerset Lifesciences Inc. (Somerset) has agreed to pay $4 million to resolve common law claims for causing Medicare Part D (Medicare) to pay for its prescription-only (Rx-only) generic drug Olopatadine when it was no longer eligible for Medicare coverage. Medicare does not cover drugs that can be purchased by retail customers over-the-counter (OTC) without a prescription. In 2020, the brand name version of Olopatadine switched from Rx-only to OTC, and Somerset was required to change Olopatadine’s label from Rx-only to OTC as well. Instead, Somerset continued to label and sell Olopatadine as Rx-only and caused Medicare to wrongfully pay claims for an OTC drug.

daedf173a6:94529064d3c46d7d.title: Owner of Health Care Software Company Sentenced to 19 Years in Prison for $1B Medicare Fraud
daedf173a6:94529064d3c46d7d.summary: A Kansas CEO and owner of an internet platform was sentenced yesterday to 19 years in prison for his role in operating a platform that generated false doctors’ orders and prescriptions to defraud Medicare and other federal health care benefit programs out of more than $1 billion.

daedf173a6:f19bd9cbe0e13677.title: Illegal Alien from Mexico Sentenced for International Conspiracy to Smuggle Aliens from Canada into United States
daedf173a6:f19bd9cbe0e13677.summary: Edgar Sanchez-Solis, 27, an illegal alien from Mexico, was sentenced today to five years in prison for his role in an international human smuggling conspiracy that illegally brought aliens from Mexico and Central and South America across the northern border with Canada into the United States.

ef78496c13:2a829ab142f8603a.title: AI subsidies as a tool for redistribution
ef78496c13:2a829ab142f8603a.author: Lucas Parmentier
ef78496c13:2a829ab142f8603a.summary: I study the optimal taxation of artificial intelligence (AI). My analysis highlights a wage-compression effect that provides a rationale for subsidizing AI, as AI adoption may reduce rather than increase wage inequality. When this effect outweighs AI's social costs, AI should be subsidized instead of taxed. I treat AI as a productive input distinct from robots, as the two technologies perform different ranges of tasks. Using numerical simulations, I demonstrate that the optimal policy for AI may differ sharply from that for robots. Under the benchmark calibration, AI is subsidized, whereas robots are taxed. Therefore, the case for taxing AI is weaker than is commonly assumed. When AI lowers the skill premium, fiscal policy may need to encourage, rather than slow, adoption.

ef78496c13:eca2edd3a3e68962.title: Illustrating long-run fiscal challenges using the Long-Term Model
ef78496c13:eca2edd3a3e68962.author: Yvan Guillemette
ef78496c13:eca2edd3a3e68962.summary: This paper presents updated estimates of long-run fiscal gaps for 35 OECD and accession candidate countries using the OECD Global Long-Term Model. The long-run fiscal gap measures the fiscal adjustment required at the 2060 horizon to keep public debt ratios stable near current levels while maintaining current service standards and benefit entitlements. The methodology incorporates several refinements, including projected increases in defence spending and a more detailed treatment of primary expenditure. In the absence of additional policy action, the median country would require a fiscal adjustment of 4.7 percentage points of GDP between 2027 and 2060 to stabilise debt, with substantially larger adjustments in some countries. Population ageing is the main driver of long-run fiscal pressures through higher pension, health and long-term care spending, compounded in many cases by weak initial fiscal positions. The paper also assesses the sensitivity of fiscal gaps to key assumptions and policy scenarios.

ef78496c13:5149234641e39737.title: Puff, Puff, Tax: Internal Revenue Code Section 280E Penalizes State-Sanctioned Marijuana Companies and Undermines the Ability-To-Pay Principle
ef78496c13:5149234641e39737.author: Thomas, Joseph E.
ef78496c13:5149234641e39737.summary: This Comment argues that Internal Revenue Code § 280E unfairly penalizes state-licensed marijuana businesses by denying ordinary business deductions and taxing them on amounts that may exceed their actual profits. Examining the history of § 280E and recent challenges by marijuana dispensaries, the Comment contends that the provision undermines the ability-to-pay principle and threatens the viability of legitimate cannabis businesses operating under state law. It concludes that Congress should amend or repeal § 280E as applied to state-sanctioned marijuana companies. [This abstract was written by Microsoft Copilot, a generative artificial intelligence.]

ef78496c13:ff7c9e7ffc66d431.title: HORIZONTAL INEQUALITY IN OPTIMALTAXATION: EVIDENCE FROM A DEVELOPMENT CONTEXT
ef78496c13:ff7c9e7ffc66d431.author: Magnus Eldrup
ef78496c13:ff7c9e7ffc66d431.summary: Exemptions are a key feature of income tax systems in developing countries, yet standard optimal tax models cannot explain them. By assuming full compliance, these models ignore horizontal inequality between formal and informal workers, understating the social cost of taxing the former. Extending the optimal tax framework, I incorporate informality and horizontal inequality aversion. I conduct a survey experiment in Kenya, finding that respondents place substantially higher welfare weight on formal taxpayers than otherwise identical informal workers. Combining these empirical preferences with administrative tax data yields prescriptions of high exemption thresholds matching observed policy, a result alternative explanations cannot rationalize.

ef78496c13:07a32f71b5767c53.title: Inheritance Taxation and the Allocation of Productive Assets in Family Firms
ef78496c13:07a32f71b5767c53.author: Roedriguez del Valle, Adrian
ef78496c13:07a32f71b5767c53.summary: We examine how taxation of intergenerational transfers affects the allocation of productive assets within family firms. Using administrative registry data on family-farm successions in Sweden around the 2005 abolition of inheritance and gift taxes, we investigate how the successor’s share of land holdings in the parental and sibling generations responds to the removal of taxes. We use a quasi-experimental event-study design and find that the increase in the successor’s ownership share is about 10–11 percentage points larger among families with greater predetermined exposure to the pre-reform inheritance tax. Results also indicate that the reform led parents to transfer assets earlier and concentrate a larger share of productive assets in the successor through inter vivos gifts. Post-reform successions are associated with higher capital intensity, suggesting that inheritance and gift taxation extends beyond the direct tax burden, affecting property-right allocation and capital intensity in family-operated enterprises.

ef78496c13:b3378300d0502c4e.title: Applying but not Receiving: Longer Working Lives and Institutionalized Health Investment
ef78496c13:b3378300d0502c4e.author: Felix Weinhardt
ef78496c13:b3378300d0502c4e.summary: Rising life expectancy and demographic change have increased the share of older workers, making their health and productivity central to aging societies. We study whether longer working lives translate into investments in work-related health before retirement. Exploiting a pension reform in Germany in a Regression Discontinuity Design, we show that women facing longer careers are more likely to apply for work-related rehabilitation, particularly those in poorer health or with weaker labor market attachment. Despite higher application and approval rates, this demand does not translate into higher rehabilitation completion. Together with intermediate outcomes, our findings are most consistent with capacity constraints in program delivery.

ef78496c13:e85df75209977206.title: How Redistributive are Public Health Care Schemes? Evidence from Medicare and Medicaid in Old Age
ef78496c13:e85df75209977206.author: McCauley, J.
ef78496c13:e85df75209977206.summary: Most health care for the US population aged 65 and older is publicly funded through Medicare and Medicaid. Despite the massive expenditures of these systems, little is known about how redistributive they are. Using data from the Health and Retirement Study, matched to administrative Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security earnings records, we estimate the distribution of lifetime Medicare and Medicaid benefits received and the distribution of lifetime taxes paid to finance these benefits. We find that benefits are greatest among the high income, largely because higher-income households live longer. Nonetheless, high income people pay more in the way of taxes. In present discounted values at age 65, households at the bottom of the income distribution gain the most from these programs, driven by high Medicaid benefits and low tax burdens. All income groups gain from these programs for the cohort we study: the lifetime tax contributions did not cover the medical benefits they received. This deficit must be paid by younger cohorts.

b0a91b96f4:7ec112c975bad06e.title: From Eyeballs to Annual Run Rates (ARR): Buzzy Pricing Metrics and the Anthropic Trade!
b0a91b96f4:7ec112c975bad06e.author: Aswath Damodaran (noreply@blogger.com)
b0a91b96f4:7ec112c975bad06e.summary: I was in San Francisco last week to talk to NYU Stern Alumni on October 15, and it was the day that Anthropic had a pre-IPO meeting with prospective investors. While I was not at the meeting, the focus of teh gathering was laying a foundation for its upcoming IPO, with the company reporting third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, which news reports described as surging 45% over the previous quarter's revenues, and positive profits, albeit on an adjusted basis. During the meeting, Anthropic also reported an annual revenue run rate (ARR) of $67 billion, a metric that those in the AI space have adopted with gusto, with an estimate that the ARR would exceed $100 billion by the end of the year. The nature of ARR, where choices on how revenue is calculated (gross versus net) and on annualization periods (daily, weekly or monthly) can make a significant difference, has led investors to be skeptical about comparing these numbers across time and companies. While I share some of that skepticism, it is worth remembering that young businesses are often priced on inventive metrics, some with more basis than others. In the late nineties, dot.com companies were priced not just on the number of visitors to their websites, but on eyeballs , where Mary Meeker argued that ad spending at these companies was correlated with time that these visitors spent on websites (eyeballs) rather than total visitors. In the last decade, you saw social media companies priced based upon the number of users and subscription-based companies on subscriber numbers. In this post, I will try to lay out the rationale for why pricing supplants valuation in young companies and why that pricing almost always has to be built around messy metrics like eyeballs, users and ARR, rather than more conventional metrics like earnings, book value or cash flows. I argued that the resilience of stocks during the year could be traced to higher-than-expected earnings being reported by companies in 2026, and a concurrent increase in expected earnings in 2027 and 2028. Now that September 2026 is one for the record books, it is time to take stock and dig a little deeper, especially since the month brought about one of the largest increase in treasury yield rates in recent memory, and stock prices still held their own. In particular, I want to examine the earnings at US companies, in the aggregate and by sector, trying to trace out where the earnings increase is coming from, and how that increased earnings is playing out on corporate balance sheets and cash flows. b0a91b96f4:13fb9371d133797f.title: Interest Rates and Stock Prices: An Old Debate Flares up!
b0a91b96f4:13fb9371d133797f.author: Aswath Damodaran (noreply@blogger.com)
b0a91b96f4:13fb9371d133797f.summary: The war in Iran, oil prices and worries about a recession have all taken turns driving stock prices in 2026 but talk about interest rates and where they are going has been a constant concern all year. In the last few weeks, interest rate worries have come to the surface again, for three reasons, all related. The first is the rise in long-term US treasury rates to levels not seen in twenty years. The second is US debt exceeding $40 trillion for the first time , bringing attention to a long-standing worry that this debt burden may be hitting a tipping point for bond buyers. The third is a that the Federal Reserve has a new chair in Kevin Warsh, and for the many Fed Watchers, who are uncertain about where he plans to lead the Fed, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting coming up in mid-September looms larger than ever. In this post, I hope to step back from the day-to-day coverage of US treasury yields and look at their performance in 2026, not only with a longer term perspective, but also in the context of movements in long terms yields in government bonds in other currencies. I also intend to revisit a discussion that I initiated in 2022, when interest rates were the central act in markets, about the relationship between interest rates and stock prices, and why higher rates do not always translate into lower stock prices, and why that effect will vary across sectors and companies. Government Borrowing Rates Governments borrow money and often do so by issuing bonds in financial markets. The rates on these bonds reflect the concerns that lenders have about the purchasing power of the currencies that they are issued in, and government bond rates, for better or worse, become indicators that drive day-to-day market movements in almost all asset classes. In this section, I will begin with an examination of US treasury rates before expanding the discussion to government bond rates in other currencies. b0a91b96f4:705ca8baf30517c9.title: The Scaling and Profitability Trade off: Venture Capital's Weakest Link!
b0a91b96f4:705ca8baf30517c9.author: Aswath Damodaran (noreply@blogger.com)
b0a91b96f4:705ca8baf30517c9.summary: It is undeniable technology companies have found their most hospitable setting in the United States and while there are many reasons for the US dominance of technology, easier access to capital for young businesses has been a key ingredient. Venture capital in the US, in its institutional and organized form, can trace its roots back to the 1950s, and over the last few decades, it has generated its share of legendary investors. Vinod Khosla is one of those legends, and it is for that reason that I was surprised to see him tweet the following: I understand that utterances on social media, often in response to comments by others or made in anger, are often quickly regretted, and I believe (though I am not certain) that Mr. Khosla did not quite mean what he said here, confusing profitability with cash flows, and arguing that every business should put scaling ahead of profitability. That said, his view that scaling should be given priority over profitability is more the norm, than the exception, among many venture capitalists, and while it probably always has been the case, I believe the tilt towards scaling has become pronounced in the last two decades. In this post, I want to zero in on the scaling and profitability trade off, how the emphasis on the former over the latter plays out at start-ups and very young companies, and why we live with the consequences, whether they want to or not. Scaling versus Business Building To put the choices you will face on scaling up versus business building into perspective, let's assume that you are a founder, and that your start-up has a tested product and that you believe there is a market for that product. You can stay with what you have built and build a business to take advantage of the immediate market, focusing on financial health and profitability. The fact that you will stay small, and perhaps unrecognized in markets other than your own, is a minus, but there are pluses. You will have little need for external capital, and…

1aa97d921e:bd2718ce7fe44e03.title: Anti-Monopoly as Industrial Policy: The Chicago School Versus Adam Smith
1aa97d921e:bd2718ce7fe44e03.author: Richard R. John
1aa97d921e:bd2718ce7fe44e03.summary: Jolted by the Great Depression of the 1930s, Thurman Arnold devised an anti-monopoly industrial policy for the United States Justice Department that breathed fresh life into a then-moribund Sherman Anti-Trust Act. Arnold’s jurisprudence built on Adam Smith’s discovery that market-making could promote national security and forestall civil unrest. Smith’s insights had informed the industrial policy of Alexander Hamilton, who laid the groundwork in the 1790s for the country’s economic development. Edward H. Levi brought Arnold’s pragmatic anti-monopolism to the University of Chicago. Here, ironically, Arnoldian jurisprudence would be transmogrified into the doctrinaire company-over-country market fundamentalism of the Chicago School of Economics. Today, writes Richard R. John, as we envision for the 21st century a new pro-market, pro-freedom, pro-national security industrial policy, it is worth recalling how U. S. economic development took the form that it did, why the Chicago School repudiated the enduring wisdom of Adam Smith, and what this portends for the world of today. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.title: How George Stigler and the Chicago School Opened the Marketplace of Ideas to Business
1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.author: Edward Nik-Khah
1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.summary: Henry Simons, the “Crown Prince” of the Chicago School and a professor in the economics department and the law school prior to World War II, sought to develop a laissez faire economics program devoted to eliminating monopoly and pursuing egalitarian goals. George Stigler and the Chicago School abandoned Simons’s anti-monopoly and egalitarian program. The best market became one driven by the search for profits, and the best-functioning marketplace of ideas arose where winning ideas reflected the greater funding backing them, writes Edward Nik-Khah. 1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.title: The Chicago School Abandoned the Positive Freedom of Adam Smith and the Founding Fathers
1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.author: Maha Rafi Atal
1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.summary: Adam Smith’s theory of political economy did not begin with the isolated individual but rather the individual who operates to earn the respect of others. Wealth and freedom grew from these relationships and engaging with others to create a free society, or what 20th century philosopher Isaiah Berlin’s would call positive freedom. In the 1970s and ‘80s, the Chicago School abandoned this aspect of freedom in preference of the isolated individual, which in turn produced a weaker concept of freedom, morality, and society that has stifled the cultivation of all three in the United States, writes Maha Rafi Atal. 1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.title: Adam Smith’s Moral Philosophy Complicates Interpretations by the Chicago School and Its Critics
1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.author: Sandra Peart and David Levy
1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.summary: The connections between Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations and Theory of Moral Sentiments reveal a much more complicated understanding of how markets work than developed in the common interpretation by the Chicago School of economics or that of its critics. Smith’s political economy based on commerce, sympathy, and competition produced social good but only when complemented and checked by other forces. When not checked, Smith worried about “factions” that produce bad outcomes, write Sandra J. Peart and David M. Levy. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:21d2bb63cb082313.summary: The post-World War II Chicago School of Aaron Director and Milton Friedman reimagined a new (neo) liberalism that treated economic liberties and the free market as the greatest defense of political rights. The government, and democracy, were more often than not barriers to economic liberties. The United States continues to suffer from neoliberalism’s prescriptions, and addressing the concerns of today’s populist movements will mean rediscovering ideas of freedom that the Chicago School denigrated, writes Robert Van Horn. 1aa97d921e:d2d33a26a587fd61.author: David Mitch
1aa97d921e:d2d33a26a587fd61.summary: The Chicago School is often associated with laissez-faire economics that reads into Adam Smith’s philosophy of political economy justifications for self-interest and prudential motivations. The early University of Chicago pursued a program that emphasized that laissez-faire economics and a concern for the public interest were not antagonists but perfectly compatible, writes David Mitch. 1aa97d921e:f1e2511bf4ba4c0f.title: America Became Rich Because of Liberalism
1aa97d921e:f1e2511bf4ba4c0f.author: Peter J. Boettke
1aa97d921e:f1e2511bf4ba4c0f.summary: Adam Smith and the Founding Fathers envisioned a society in which economic and political freedom, grouped together in the ideology of liberalism, would produce a wealthy, free, and peaceful society. Centuries later, this vision has come to fruition, and F. A. Hayek and Milton Friedman helped elaborate and advance that vision in their economic and philosophical works. The lesson for today’s populist moment is not to abandon these principles, but to continue to pursue them, as it is their imperfect realization, not their imperfect conceptualization, that burdens today’s society, writes Peter Boettke.
